entries.edbe076ea17e633d8744d41664ff382488da1d68: <div sID="gen14514" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="27" osisID="Prov.27" sID="Prov.27"/> <div eID="gen14514" type="x-p"/>
entries.66049ee616792606d2fb56d4d25dcd666751d2fd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv83"/><title type="x-s3">Miscellaneous Maxims.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv83"/> <div sID="gen14515" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth. <div eID="gen14515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14516" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A good caution against presuming upon time to come: <hi type="italic">Boast not thyself,</hi> no, not <hi type="italic">of to-morrow,</hi> much less of many days or years to come. This does not forbid preparing for to-morrow, but presuming upon to-morrow. We must not promise ourselves the continuance of our lives and comforts till to-morrow, but speak of it with submission to the will of God and as those who with good reason are kept at uncertainty about it. We must not <hi type="italic">take thought for the morrow</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.34">Matt. vi. 34</reference>), but we must cast our care concerning it upon God. See <reference osisRef="Jas.4.13-Jas.4.15">James iv. 13-15</reference>. We must not put off the great work of conversion, that one thing needful, till to-morrow, as if we were sure of it, <hi type="italic">but to-day, while it is called to-day,</hi> hear God's voice. 2. A good consideration, upon which this caution is grounded: <hi type="italic">We know not what a day may bring forth,</hi> what event may be in the teeming womb, of time; it is a secret till it is born, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.5">Eccl. xi. 5</reference>. A little time may produce considerable changes, and such as we little think of. We <hi type="italic">know not what</hi> the present <hi type="italic">day may bring forth;</hi> the evening must commend it. <hi type="italic">Nescis quid serus vesper vehat—Thou knowest not what the close of evening may bring with it.</hi> God has wisely kept us in the dark concerning future events, and reserved to himself the knowledge of them, as a flower of the crown, that he may train us up in a dependence upon himself and a continued readiness for every event, <reference osisRef="Acts.1.7">Acts i. 7</reference>.
entries.9391b9af9a2322cb119751d0d1b549fe46f46f6e: <div eID="gen14516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14517" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thine own lips. <div eID="gen14517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14518" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. We must do that which is commendable, for which even strangers may praise us. Our <hi type="italic">light</hi> must <hi type="italic">shine before men,</hi> and we must do good works that may be seen, though we must not do them on purpose that they may be seen. Let our own works be such as will praise us, even <hi type="italic">in the gates,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.8">Phil. iv. 8</reference>. 2. When we have done it we must not commend ourselves, for that is an evidence of pride, folly, and self-love, and a great lessening to a man's reputation. Every one will be forward to run him down that cries himself up. There may be a just occasion for us to vindicate ourselves, but it does not become us to applaud ourselves. <hi type="italic">Proprio laus sordet in ore—Self-praise defiles the mouth.</hi>
entries.787955037649e6f6fbb1f404687640a65ef1679b: <div eID="gen14518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14519" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> A stone <hi type="italic">is</hi> heavy, and the sand weighty; but a fool's wrath <hi type="italic">is</hi> heavier than them both. <hi type="super">4</hi> Wrath <hi type="italic">is</hi> cruel, and anger <hi type="italic">is</hi> outrageous; but who <hi type="italic">is</hi> able to stand before envy? <div eID="gen14519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14520" type="x-p"/> These two verses show the intolerable mischief, 1. Of ungoverned passion. The wrath of a fool, who when he is provoked cares not what he says and does, is more grievous than a great stone or a load of sand. It lies heavily upon himself. Those who have no command of their passions do themselves even sink under the load of them. The wrath of a fool lies heavily upon those he is enraged at, to whom, in his fury, he will be in danger of doing some mischief. It is therefore our wisdom not to give provocation to a fool, but, if he be in a passion, to get out of his way. 2. Of rooted malice, which is as much worse than the former as coals of juniper are worse than a fire of thorns. <hi type="italic">Wrath</hi> (it is true) <hi type="italic">is cruel,</hi> and does many a barbarous thing, <hi type="italic">and anger is outrageous;</hi> but a secret enmity at the person of another, an envy at his prosperity, and a desire of revenge for some injury or affront, are much more mischievous. One may avoid a sudden heat, as David escaped Saul's javelin, but when it grows, as Saul's did, to a settled envy, there is no <hi type="italic">standing before it;</hi> it will pursue; it will overtake. He that grieves at the good of another will be still contriving to do him hurt, and will keep his anger for ever.
entries.00c6375fc8ed058dbc7810bde39fd9bb8abb5bc6: <div eID="gen14520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14521" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Open rebuke <hi type="italic">is</hi> better than secret love. 6 Faithful <hi type="italic">are</hi> the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy <hi type="italic">are</hi> deceitful. <div eID="gen14521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14522" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is good for us to be reproved, and told of our faults, by our friends. If true love in the heart has but zeal and courage enough to show itself in dealing plainly with our friends, and reproving them for what they say and do amiss, this is really <hi type="italic">better,</hi> not only than secret hatred (as <reference osisRef="Lev.19.17">Lev. xix. 17</reference>), but <hi type="italic">than secret love,</hi> that love to our neighbours which does not show itself in this good fruit, which compliments them in their sins, to the prejudice of their souls. <hi type="italic">Faithful are the reproofs of a friend,</hi> though for the present they are painful as <hi type="italic">wounds.</hi> It is a sign that our friends are faithful indeed if, in love to our souls, they will not suffer sin upon us, nor let us alone in it. The physician's care is to cure the patient's disease, not to please his palate. 2. It is dangerous to be caressed and flattered by <hi type="italic">an enemy,</hi> whose <hi type="italic">kisses are deceitful</hi> We can take no pleasure in them because we can put no confidence in them (Joab's kiss and Judas's were deceitful), and therefore we have need to stand upon our guard, that we be not deluded by them; they are to be deprecated. Some read it: <hi type="italic">The Lord deliver us from an enemy's kisses, from lying lips, and from a deceitful tongue.</hi>
entries.2cf2b99294feb939fd40c2f49fdbe79f9e781b5f: <div eID="gen14522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14523" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> The full soul loatheth an honeycomb; but to the hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet. <div eID="gen14523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14524" type="x-p"/> Solomon here, as often in this book, shows that the poor have in some respects the advantage of the rich; for, 1. They have a better relish of their enjoyments than the rich have. Hunger is the best sauce. Coarse fare, with a good appetite to it has a sensible pleasantness in it, which those are strangers to whose hearts are <hi type="italic">overcharged with surfeiting.</hi> Those that fare sumptuously every day nauseate even delicate food, as the Israelites did the quails; whereas those that have no more than their necessary food, though it be such as <hi type="italic">the full soul</hi> would call <hi type="italic">bitter,</hi> to them it <hi type="italic">is sweet;</hi> they eat it with pleasure, digest it, and are refreshed by it. 2. They are more thankful for their enjoyments: <hi type="italic">The hungry</hi> will bless God for bread and water, while those that are <hi type="italic">full</hi> think the greatest dainties and varieties scarcely worth giving thanks for. The virgin Mary seems to refer to this when she says (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.53">Luke i. 53</reference>), <hi type="italic">The hungry,</hi> who know how to value God's blessings, <hi type="italic">are filled with good things,</hi> but <hi type="italic">the rich,</hi> who despise them, are justly <hi type="italic">sent empty away.</hi>
entries.e84e7306d48258a74d0bb447fd92c5452ec92b1e: <div eID="gen14524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14525" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> As a bird that wandereth from her nest, so <hi type="italic">is</hi> a man that wandereth from his place. <div eID="gen14525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14526" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. There are many that do not know when they are well off, but are uneasy with their present condition, and given to change. God, in his providence, has appointed them a place fit for them and has made it comfortable to them; but they affect unsettledness; they love to wander; they are glad of a pretence to go abroad, and do not care for staying long at a place; they needlessly absent themselves from their own work and care, and meddle with that which belongs not to them. 2. Those that thus desert the post assigned to them are like <hi type="italic">a bird that wanders from her nest.</hi> It is an instance of their folly; they are like a silly bird; they are always wavering, like the wandering bird that hops from bough to bough and rests nowhere. It is unsafe; the bird that wanders is exposed; a man's place is his castle; he that quits it makes himself an easy prey to the fowler. When the bird wanders from her nest the eggs and young ones there are neglected. Those that love to be abroad leave their work at home undone. <hi type="italic">Let every man therefore, in the calling wherein he is called, therein abide,</hi> therein abide <hi type="italic">with God.</hi>
entries.840f0454b0f3af2db4660fe8969bbf4cbdf06920: <div eID="gen14526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14527" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Ointment and perfume rejoice the heart: so <hi type="italic">doth</hi> the sweetness of a man's friend by hearty counsel. 10 Thine own friend, and thy father's friend, forsake not; neither go into thy brother's house in the day of thy calamity: <hi type="italic">for</hi> better <hi type="italic">is</hi> a neighbour <hi type="italic">that is</hi> near than a brother far off. <div eID="gen14527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14528" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A charge given to be faithful and constant to our friends, our old friends, to keep up an intimacy with them, and to be ready to do them all the offices that lie in our power. It is good to have a friend, a bosom-friend, whom we can be free with, and with whom we may communicate counsels. It is not necessary that this friend should be a relation, or any way akin to us, though it is happiest when, among those who are so, we find one fit to make a friend of. Peter and Andrew were brethren, so were James and John; yet Solomon frequently distinguishes between a friend and a brother. But it is advisable to choose a friend among our neighbours who live near us, that acquaintance may be kept up and kindnesses the more frequently interchanged. It is good also to have a special respect to those who have been friends to our family: "<hi type="italic">Thy own friend,</hi> especially if he have been <hi type="italic">thy father's friend, forsake not;</hi> fail not both to serve him and to use him, as there is occasion. He is a tried friend; he knows thy affairs; he has a particular concern for thee; therefore be advised by him." It is a duty we owe to our parents, when they are gone, to love their friends and consult with them. Solomon's son undid himself by forsaking the counsel of his father's friends. 2. A good reason given why we should thus value true friendship and be choice of it. (1.) Because of the pleasure of it. There is a great deal of <hi type="italic">sweetness</hi> in conversing and consulting with a cordial friend. It is like <hi type="italic">ointment and perfume,</hi> which are very grateful to the smell, and exhilarate the spirits. It <hi type="italic">rejoices the heart;</hi> the burden of care is made lighter by unbosoming ourselves to our friend, and it is a great satisfaction to us to have his sentiments concerning our affairs. <hi type="italic">The sweetness of</hi> friendship lies not in hearty mirth, and hearty laughter, but in <hi type="italic">hearty counsel,</hi> faithful advice, sincerely given and without flattery, <hi type="italic">by counsel of the soul</hi> (so the word is), counsel which reaches the case, and comes to the heart, counsel about soul-concerns, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.16">Ps. lxvi. 16</reference>. We should reckon that the most pleasant conversation which is about spiritual things, and promotes the prosperity of the soul. (2.) Because of the profit and advantage of it, especially in a <hi type="italic">day of calamity.</hi> We are here advised not to go into a <hi type="italic">brother's house,</hi> not to expect relief from a kinsman merely for kindred-sake, for the obligation of that commonly goes little further than calling cousin and fails when it comes to the trial of a real kindness, but rather to apply ourselves to our neighbours, who are at hand, and will be ready to help us at an exigence. It is wisdom to oblige them by being neighbourly, and we shall have the benefit of it in distress, by finding them so to us, <reference osisRef="Prov.18.24">ch. xviii. 24</reference>.
entries.8a77866384c1f38fff55834d1aedef4bbca27f7c: <div eID="gen14528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14529" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> My son, be wise, and make my heart glad, that I may answer him that reproacheth me. <div eID="gen14529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14530" type="x-p"/> Children are here exhorted to be wise and good, 1. That they may be a comfort to their parents and may <hi type="italic">make their hearts glad,</hi> even when <hi type="italic">the evil days come,</hi> and so recompense them for their care, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.15">ch. xxiii. 15</reference>. 2. That they may be a credit to them: "<hi type="italic">That I may answer him that reproaches me</hi> with having been over-strict and severe in bringing up my children, and having taken a wrong method with them in restraining them from the liberties which other young people take. <hi type="italic">My son, be wise,</hi> and then it will appear, in the effect, that I went the wisest way to work with my children." Those that have been blessed with a religious education should in every thing conduct themselves so as to be a credit to their education and to silence those who say, <hi type="italic">A young saint, an old devil;</hi> and to prove the contrary, <hi type="italic">A young saint, an old angel.</hi>
entries.4896f2729efa5722ec07966cdb1dfec0624df934: <div eID="gen14530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14531" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> A prudent <hi type="italic">man</hi> foreseeth the evil, <hi type="italic">and</hi> hideth himself; <hi type="italic">but</hi> the simple pass on, <hi type="italic">and</hi> are punished. <div eID="gen14531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14532" type="x-p"/> This we had before, <reference osisRef="Prov.22.3">ch. xxii. 3</reference>. Note, 1. Evil may be foreseen. Where there is temptation, it is easy to foresee that if we thrust ourselves into it there will be sin, and as easy to foresee that if we venture upon the evil of sin there will follow the evil of punishment; and, commonly, God warns before he wounds, having <hi type="italic">set watchmen over us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.6.17">Jer. vi. 17</reference>. 2. It will be well or ill with us according as we do or do not improve the foresight we have of evil before us: The <hi type="italic">prudent man, foreseeing the evil,</hi> forecasts accordingly, <hi type="italic">and hides himself, but the simple</hi> is either so dull that he does not foresee it or so wilful and slothful that he will take no care to avoid it, and so he <hi type="italic">passes on</hi> securely <hi type="italic">and is punished.</hi> We do well for ourselves when we provide for hereafter.
entries.cd0a1dbcf86dfae238ed29b13cf0fc3ddc17a0c2: <div eID="gen14532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14533" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> Take his garment that is surety for a stranger, and take a pledge of him for a strange woman. <div eID="gen14533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14534" type="x-p"/> This also we had before, <reference osisRef="Prov.20.16">ch. xx. 16</reference>. 1. It shows who those are that are hastening to poverty, those that have so little consideration as to be bound for every body that will ask them and those that are given to women. Such as these will take up money as far as ever their credit will go, but they will certainly cheat their creditors at last, nay, they are cheating them all along. An honest man may be made a beggar, but he is not honest that makes himself one. 2. It advises us to be so discreet in ordering our affairs as not to lend money to those who are manifestly wasting their estates, unless they give very good security for it. Foolish lending is injustice to our families. He does not say, "Get another to be bound with him," for he that makes himself a common voucher will have those to be his security who are as insolvent as himself; therefore <hi type="italic">take his garment.</hi>
entries.3f320fce3eab3eae4f88ce59f216df353b2a011e: <div eID="gen14534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14535" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> He that blesseth his friend with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, it shall be counted a curse to him. <div eID="gen14535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14536" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is a great folly to be extravagant in praising even the best of our friends and benefactors. It is our duty to give every one his due praise, to applaud those who excel in knowledge, virtue, and usefulness, and to acknowledge the kindnesses we have received with thankfulness; but to do this <hi type="italic">with a loud voice, rising early in the morning,</hi> to be always harping on this string, in all companies, even to our friend's face, or so as that he may be sure to hear it, to do it studiously, as we do that which we rise early to, to magnify the merits of our friend above measure and with hyperboles, is fulsome, and nauseous, and savours of hypocrisy and design. Praising men for what they have done is only to get more out of them; and every body concludes the parasite hopes to be well paid for his panegyric or epistle dedicatory. We must not give that praise to our friend which is due to God only, as some think is intimated in <hi type="italic">rising early</hi> to do it; for in the morning God is to be praised. We must not <hi type="italic">make too much haste to praise men</hi> (so some understand it), not cry up men too soon for their abilities and performances, but let them first be proved; lest they be lifted up with pride, and laid to sleep in idleness. 2. It is a greater folly to be fond of being ourselves extravagantly praised. A wise man rather counts it <hi type="italic">a curse,</hi> and a reflection upon him, not only designed to pick his pocket, but which may really turn to his prejudice. Modest praises (as a great man observes) invite such as are present to add to the commendation, but immodest immoderate praises tempt them to detract rather, and to censure one that they hear over-commended. And, besides, over-praising a man makes him the object of envy; every man puts in for a share of reputation, and therefore reckons himself injured if another monopolize it or have more given him than his share. And the greatest danger of all is that it is a temptation to pride; men are apt to think of themselves above what is meet when others speak of them above what is meet. See how careful blessed Paul was not to be over-valued, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.6">2 Cor. xii. 6</reference>.
entries.e76b0c3b83fd6ac46f3e43b8bb1f8672b5f367a7: <div eID="gen14536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14537" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> A continual dropping in a very rainy day and a contentious woman are alike. <hi type="super">16</hi> Whosoever hideth her hideth the wind, and the ointment of his right hand, <hi type="italic">which</hi> bewrayeth <hi type="italic">itself.</hi> <div eID="gen14537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14538" type="x-p"/> Here, as before, Solomon laments the case of him that has a peevish passionate wife, that is continually chiding, and making herself and all about her uneasy. 1. It is a grievance that there is no avoiding, for it is like <hi type="italic">a continual dropping in a very rainy day.</hi> The contentions of a neighbour may be like a sharp shower, troublesome for the time, yet, while it lasts, one may take shelter; but <hi type="italic">the contentions of a wife</hi> are like a constant soaking rain, for which there is no remedy but patience See <reference osisRef="Prov.19.13">ch. xix. 13</reference>. 2. It is a grievance that there is no concealing. A wise man would hide it if he could, for the sake both of his own and his wife's reputation, but he cannot, any more than he can conceal the noise of the wind when it blows or the smell of a strong perfume. Those that are froward and brawling will proclaim their own shame, even when their friends, in kindness to them, would cover it.
entries.0429d400d20475e12468259497aec4bae1a8410f: <div eID="gen14538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14539" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend. <div eID="gen14539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14540" type="x-p"/> This intimates both the pleasure and the advantage of conversation. One man is nobody; nor will poring upon a book in a corner accomplish a man as the reading and studying of men will. Wise and profitable discourse sharpens men's wits; and those that have ever so much knowledge may by conference have something added to them. It sharpens men's looks, and, by cheering the spirits, puts a briskness and liveliness into the countenance, and gives a man such an air as shows he is pleased himself and makes him pleasing to those about him. Good men's graces are sharpened by converse with those that are good, and bad men's lusts and passions are sharpened by converse with those that are bad, as iron is sharpened by its like, especially by the file. Men are filed, made smooth, and bright, and fit for business (who were rough, and dull, and inactive), by conversation. This is designed, 1. To recommend to us this expedient for sharpening ourselves, but with a caution to take heed whom we choose to converse with, because the influence upon us is so great either for the better or for the worse. 2. To direct us what we must have in our eye in conversation, namely to improve both others and ourselves, not to pass away time or banter one another, but to <hi type="italic">provoke one another to love and to good works</hi> and so to make one another wiser and better.
entries.6b32b8dea752ff6bce7ee6e6408eb18213d52c32: <div eID="gen14540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14541" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Whoso keepeth the fig tree shall eat the fruit thereof: so he that waiteth on his master shall be honoured. <div eID="gen14541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14542" type="x-p"/> This is designed to encourage diligence, faithfulness, and constancy, even in mean employments. Though the calling be laborious and despicable, yet those who keep to it will find there is something to be got by it. 1. Let not a poor gardener, who <hi type="italic">keeps the fig-tree,</hi> be discouraged; though it require constant care and attendance to nurse up fig-trees, and, when they have grown to maturity, to keep them in good order, and gather the figs in their season, yet he shall be paid for his pains: He <hi type="italic">shall eat the fruit</hi> of it, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.7">1 Cor. ix. 7</reference>. 2. Nay, let not a poor servant think himself incapable of thriving and being preferred; for if he be diligent in <hi type="italic">waiting on his master,</hi> observant of him and obedient to him, if <hi type="italic">he keep his master</hi> (so the word is), if he do all he can for the securing of his person and reputation and take care that his estate be not wasted or damaged, such a one <hi type="italic">shall be honoured,</hi> shall not only get a good word, but be preferred and rewarded. God is a Master who has engaged to put an honour on those that serve him faithfully, <reference osisRef="John.12.26">John xii. 26</reference>.
entries.cd4c8bba80d182c240bbed1779ba6a669fc654f1: <div eID="gen14542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14543" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> As in water face <hi type="italic">answereth</hi> to face, so the heart of man to man. <div eID="gen14543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14544" type="x-p"/> This shows us that there is a way, 1. Of knowing ourselves. As the water is a looking-glass in which we may see our faces by reflection, so there are mirrors by which the <hi type="italic">heart of a man</hi> is discovered to <hi type="italic">a man,</hi> that is, to himself. Let a man examine his own conscience, his thoughts, affections, and intentions. Let him behold his <hi type="italic">natural face in the glass</hi> of the divine law (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.23">Jam. i. 23</reference>), and he may discern what kind of man he is and what is his true character, which it will be of great use to every man rightly to know. 2. Of knowing one another by ourselves; for, as there is a similitude between the face of a man and the reflection of it in the water, so there is between one man's heart and another's for God has fashioned men's hearts alike; and in many cases we may judge of others by ourselves, which is one of the foundations on which that rule is built of doing to others as we would be done by, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.9">Exod. xxiii. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">Nihil est unum uni tam simile, tam par, quam omnes inter nosmet ipsos sumus. Sui nemo ipse tam similis quam omnes sunt omnium—No one thing is so like another as man is to man. No person is so like himself as each person is to all besides. Cic. de Legib. lib.</hi> 1. One corrupt heart is like another, and so is one sanctified heart, for the former bears the same image of the earthy, the latter the same image of the heavenly.
entries.eba70934cb33814177c4e11db89e4de43ccbb3ae: <div eID="gen14544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14545" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Hell and destruction are never full; so the eyes of man are never satisfied. <div eID="gen14545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14546" type="x-p"/> Two things are here said to be insatiable, and they are two things near of kin—death and sin. 1. Death is insatiable. The first death, the second death, both are so. The grave is not clogged with the multitude of dead bodies that are daily thrown into it, but is still an <hi type="italic">open sepulchre,</hi> and cries, <hi type="italic">Give, give.</hi> Hell also has enlarged itself, and still has room for the damned spirits that are committed to that prison. <hi type="italic">Tophet is deep and large,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Isa. xxx. 33</reference>. 2. Sin is insatiable: <hi type="italic">The eyes of man are never satisfied,</hi> nor the appetites of the carnal mind towards profit or pleasure. The <hi type="italic">eye is not satisfied with seeing,</hi> nor is he the <hi type="italic">loves silver satisfied with silver.</hi> Men labour for that which surfeits, but satisfies not; nay, it is dissatisfying; but satisfies not; nay, it is dissatisfying; such a perpetual uneasiness have men justly been doomed to ever since our first parents were not satisfied with all the trees of Eden, but they must meddle with the forbidden tree. Those whose eyes are ever toward the Lord in him are satisfied, and shall for ever be so.
entries.ef677e780ba092592297baade886f4b3d1682d8e: <div eID="gen14546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14547" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> <hi type="italic">As</hi> the fining pot for silver, and the furnace for gold; so <hi type="italic">is</hi> a man to his praise. <div eID="gen14547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14548" type="x-p"/> This gives us a touchstone by which we may try ourselves. Silver and gold are tried by putting them into the furnace and fining-pot; so is man tried by praising him. Let him be extolled and preferred, and then he will show himself what he is. 1. If a man be made, by the applause that is given him, proud, conceited, and scornful,—if he take the glory to himself which he should transmit to God, as Herod did,—if, the more he is praised, the more careless he is of what he says and does,—if he <hi type="italic">lie in bed till noon</hi> because <hi type="italic">his name is up,</hi> thereby it will appear that he is a vain foolish man, and a man who, though he be praised, has nothing in him truly praise-worthy. 2. If, on the contrary, a man is made by his praise more thankful to God, more respectful to his friends, more watchful against every thing that may blemish his reputation, more diligent to improve himself, and do good to others, that he may answer the expectations of his friends from him, by this it will appear that he is a wise and good man. He has a good temper of mind who knows how to pass by evil report and good report, and is still the same, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.8">2 Cor. vi. 8</reference>.
entries.2421d0dd2df30307094522a2aa58c80a6f4f42f5: <div eID="gen14548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14549" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Though thou shouldest bray a fool in a mortar among wheat with a pestle, <hi type="italic">yet</hi> will not his foolishness depart from him. <div eID="gen14549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14550" type="x-p"/> Solomon had said (<reference osisRef="Prov.22.15">ch. xxii. 15</reference>), <hi type="italic">The foolishness</hi> which <hi type="italic">is bound in the heart of a child may be driven out by the rod of correction,</hi> for then the mind is to be moulded, the vicious habits not having taken root; but here he shows that, if it be not done then, it will be next to impossible to do it afterwards; if the disease be inveterate, there is a danger of its being incurable. <hi type="italic">Can the Ethiopian change his skin?</hi> Observe, 1. Some are so bad that rough and severe methods must be used with them, after gentle means have been tried in vain; they must be <hi type="italic">brayed in a mortar.</hi> God will take this way with them by his judgments; the magistrates must take this way with them by the rigour of the law. Force must be used with those that will not be ruled by reason, and love, and their own interest. 2. Some are so incorrigibly bad that even those rough and severe methods do not answer the end, their <hi type="italic">foolishness will not depart from them,</hi> so fully are their <hi type="italic">hearts set in them to do evil;</hi> they are often under the rod and yet not humbled, in the furnace and yet not refined, but, like Ahaz, trespass yet more (<reference osisRef="2Chr.28.22">2 Chron. xxviii. 22</reference>); and what remains then but that they should be rejected as reprobate silver?  <div eID="gen14550" type="x-p"/>
entries.5f1204eb6e7d4a2b0f5a74c2ca2cefa5322ee566: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv84"/><title type="x-s3">The Reward of Prudence.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv84"/> <div sID="gen14551" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, <hi type="italic">and</hi> look well to thy herds. <hi type="super">24</hi> For riches <hi type="italic">are</hi> not for ever: and doth the crown <hi type="italic">endure</hi> to every generation? <hi type="super">25</hi> The hay appeareth, and the tender grass sheweth itself, and herbs of the mountains are gathered. <hi type="super">26</hi> The lambs <hi type="italic">are</hi> for thy clothing, and the goats <hi type="italic">are</hi> the price of the field. <hi type="super">27</hi> And <hi type="italic">thou shalt have</hi> goats' milk enough for thy food, for the food of thy household, and <hi type="italic">for</hi> the maintenance for thy maidens. <div eID="gen14551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14552" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A command given us to be diligent in our callings. It is directed to husbandmen and shepherds, and those that deal in cattle, but it is to be extended to all other lawful callings; whatever our business is, within doors or without, we must apply our minds to it. This command intimates, 1. That we ought to have some business to do in this world and not to live in idleness. 2. We ought rightly and fully to understand our business, and know what we have to do, and not meddle with that which we do not understand. 3. We ought to have an eye to it ourselves, and not turn over all the care of it to others. We should, with our own eyes, inspect the <hi type="italic">state of our flocks,</hi> it is the master's eye that makes them fat. 4. We must be discreet and considerate in the management of our business, <hi type="italic">know the state</hi> of things, and <hi type="italic">look well</hi> to them, that nothing may be lost, no opportunity let slip, but every thing done in proper time and order, and so as to turn to the best advantage. 5. We must be <hi type="italic">diligent</hi> and take pains; not only sit down and contrive, but be up and doing: "Set thy heart to thy herds, as one in care; lay thy hands, lay thy bones, to thy business." <div eID="gen14552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14553" type="x-p"/> II. The reasons to enforce this command. Consider, <div eID="gen14553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14554" type="x-p"/> 1. The uncertainty of worldly wealth (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">Riches are not for ever.</hi> (1.) Other riches are not so durable as these are: "<hi type="italic">Look well to thy flocks and herds,</hi> thy estate in the country and the stock upon that, for these are staple commodities, which, in a succession, will be for ever, whereas riches in trade and merchandise will not be so; the <hi type="italic">crown</hi> itself may perhaps not be so sure to thy family as thy flocks and herds." (2.) Even these riches will go to decay if they be not well looked after. If a man had <hi type="italic">an abbey</hi> (as we say), and were slothful and wasteful, he might make an end of it. Even the crown and the revenues of it, if care be not taken, will suffer damage, nor will it <hi type="italic">continue to every generation</hi> without very good management. Though David had the crown entailed on his family, yet he <hi type="italic">looked well to his flocks,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.29">1 Chron. xxvii. 29</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.31">31</reference>. <div eID="gen14554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14555" type="x-p"/> 2. The bounty and liberality of nature, or rather of the God of nature, and his providence (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">The hay appears.</hi> In taking care of the <hi type="italic">flocks and herds,</hi> (1.) "There needs no great labour, no ploughing or sowing; the food for them is the spontaneous product of the ground; thou hast nothing to do but to turn them into it in the summer, <hi type="italic">when the grass shows itself,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">gather the herbs of the mountains</hi> for them against winter. God has done his part; thou art ungrateful to him, and unjustly refusest to serve his providence, if thou dost not do thine." (2.) "There is an opportunity to be observed and improved, a time when <hi type="italic">the hay appears;</hi> but, if thou let slip that time, thy flocks and herds will fare the worse for it. As for ourselves, so for our cattle, we ought, with the ant, to provide meat in summer." <div eID="gen14555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14556" type="x-p"/> 3. The profit of good husbandry in a family: "Keep thy sheep, and thy sheep will help to keep thee; thou shalt have food for thy children and servants, <hi type="italic">goats' milk enough</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.27">v. 27</reference>); and <hi type="italic">enough is as good as a feast.</hi> Thou shalt have raiment likewise: the <hi type="italic">lambs' wool shall be for thy clothing.</hi> Thou shalt have money to pay thy rent; the goats thou shalt have to sell shall be <hi type="italic">the price of thy field;</hi>" nay, as some understand it, "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt become a purchaser,</hi> and buy land to leave to thy children," (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.26">v. 26</reference>). Note, (1.) If we have food and raiment, and wherewithal to give every body his own, we have enough, and ought to be not only content, but thankful. (2.) Masters of families must provide not only for themselves, but for their families, and see that their servants have a fitting maintenance. (3.) Plain food and plain clothing, if they be but competent, are all we should aim at. "Reckon thyself well done to if thou be clothed with home-spun cloth with the fleece of thy own lambs, and fed with goats' milk; let that serve for thy food which serves for the <hi type="italic">food of thy household and the maintenance of thy maidens.</hi> Be not desirous of dainties, <hi type="italic">far-fetched and dear-bought.</hi>" (4.) This should encourage us to be careful and industrious about our business, that that will bring in a sufficient maintenance for our families; we shall <hi type="italic">eat the labour of our hands.</hi>  <chapter eID="Prov.27"/> <div eID="gen14556" type="x-p"/>

entries.c91ca14e77b707deafceaa89486dd469bed8bec2: <div eID="gen24850" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen24851" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24852" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24852" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24851" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24853" type="x-p"/> To-morrow is uncertain. Self-praise forbidden. Anger and envy. Reproof from a friend. Want makes us feel the value of a supply. A good neighbor. Beware of suretyship. Suspicious praise. The quarrelsome woman. One friend helps another. Man insatiable. The incorrigible fool. Domestic cares. The profit of flocks for food and raiment. <div eID="gen24853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24854" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen24854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24855" type="x-p"/> Boast not thyself of to-morrow - See note on <reference osisRef="Jam.4.13">Jam 4:13</reference>, etc. Do not depend on any future moment for spiritual good which at present thou needest, and God is willing to give, and without which, should death surprise thee, thou must be eternally lost; such as repentance, faith in Christ, the pardon of sin, the witness of the Holy Spirit, and complete renovation of soul. Be incessant in thy application to God for these blessings. <div eID="gen24855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24856" type="x-p"/> My old MS. Bible translates thus: Ne glorie thou into the morewenning. Here we see the derivation of our word morning; morewenning, from more, and wen or won, to dwelt, i.e., a continuance of time to live or dwell in your present habitation. Every man wishes to live longer, and therefore wishes for to-morrow; and when to-morrow comes, then to-morrow, and so on.
entries.9b4d491909e2ff55657ef748fca390684f833787: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen24856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24857" type="x-p"/> Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth - We have a similar proverb, which illustrates this: "Self-praise is no commendation."
entries.436c5b91b089eb521dbb89fbb57fbe19a6466e3f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen24857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24858" type="x-p"/> Who is able to stand before envy? - The rabbins have a curious story on this subject, and it has been formed by the moderns into a fable. There were two persons, one covetous and the other envious, to whom a certain person promised to grant whatever they should ask; but double to him who should ask last. The covetous man would not ask first, because he wished to get the double portion, and the envious man would not make the first request because he could not bear the thoughts of thus benefiting his neighbor. However, at last he requested that one of his eyes should be taken out, in order that his neighbor might lose both.
entries.5b2a1a0ae46acfed2a92239002716b8e64f8b9f1: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen24858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24859" type="x-p"/> Open rebuke is better than secret love - Plutarch gives an account of a man who, aiming a blow at his enemy's life, cut open an imposthume, which by a salutary discharge saved his life, that was sinking under a disease for which a remedy could not be found. Partial friendship covers faults; envy, malice, and revenge, will exhibit, heighten, and even multiply them. The former conceals us from ourselves; the latter shows us the worst part of our character. Thus we are taught the necessity of amendment and correction. In this sense open rebuke is better than secret love. Yet it is a rough medicine, and none can desire it. But the genuine open-hearted friend may be intended, who tells you your faults freely but conceals them from all others; hence the sixth verse: "Faithful are the wounds of a friend."
entries.9e77dd9546e23ebe461d4ae5c87e2979858b3295: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen24859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24860" type="x-p"/> Is a bird that wandereth from her nest - Leaving her own brood, places of retreat, and feeding-ground behind, and going into strange countries, where she is exposed to every kind of danger. So is the man who leaves his family connections and country, and goes into strange parts to find employment, better his circumstances, make a fortune, etc. I have seen multitudes of such wanderers from their place come to great misery and wretchedness. God's general advice is, "Do good, and dwell in the land; and verily thou shalt be fed."
entries.75b826437b9abb56e03d6f4192cf9d5e2d450908: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen24860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24861" type="x-p"/> Ointment and perfume - Anointing the head and various parts of the body with aromatic oil is frequent in the East, and fumigating the beards of the guests at the conclusion of an entertainment is almost universal; as is also sprinkling rose-water, and water highly ordoriferous. Two of the curious vessels which are used for this purpose are now before me; they hold some quarts each, and are beautifully inlaid with silver in the form of sprigs, leaves, etc.
entries.7ad59f520b131b0c84a34a35006bcad05041de8b: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen24861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24862" type="x-p"/> Thine own friend - A well and long tried friend is invaluable. Him that has been a friend to thy family never forget, and never neglect. And, in the time of adversity, rather apply to such a one, than go to thy nearest relative, who keeps himself at a distance.
entries.80f7afdeccd128df05fc373a808df7600993f9c3: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen24862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24863" type="x-p"/> A prudent man foreseeth the evil - The very same as <reference osisRef="Pro.22.3">Pro 22:3</reference>.
entries.0a81f409d1d8422985bc90538191683344f2e195: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen24863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24864" type="x-p"/> Take his garment - The same as <reference osisRef="Pro.20.16">Pro 20:16</reference>.
entries.deb0496b3b868d0ea184fd68390d9adf4ea8dab4: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen24864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24865" type="x-p"/> He that blesseth his friend - He who makes loud and public protestations of acknowledgments to his friend for favors received, subjects his sincerity to suspicion; and remember the Italian proverb elsewhere quoted: - "He who praises you more than he was wont to do, has either deceived you, or is about to do it." Extravagant public professions are little to be regarded.
entries.85daf6db8b1a788d94470a9dcb071596ce7bfb65: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen24865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24866" type="x-p"/> A continual dropping - See <reference osisRef="Pro.19.13">Pro 19:13</reference>.
entries.1d1fa0b5f54c158c59461991f98d7d0ab86dc895: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen24866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24867" type="x-p"/> Whosoever hideth her hideth the wind - You may as well attempt to repress the blowing of the wind, as the tongue of a scold; and to conceal this unfortunate propensity of a wife is as impossible as to hush the storm, and prevent its sound from being heard. <div eID="gen24867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24868" type="x-p"/> The ointment of his right hand - You can no more conceal such a woman's conduct, than you can the smell of the aromatic oil with which your hand has been anointed. The Hebrew is very obscure, and is variously translated. Coverdale thus: "He that refrayneth her, refrayneth the wynde; and holdith oyle fast in his honde." That is, he attempts to do what is impossible to be done.
entries.6ea36c908bbd327bf1823e231b868c59894ac86f: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen24868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24869" type="x-p"/> Iron sharpeneth iron - As hard iron, viz., steel, will bring a knife to a better edge when it is properly whetted against it: so one friend may be the means of exciting another to reflect, dive deeply into, and illustrate a subject, without which whetting or excitement, this had never taken place. Had Horace seen this proverb in the Septuagint translation when he wrote to the Pisos? <div eID="gen24869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24870" type="x-p"/> Ergo fungar vice cotis, acutum <div eID="gen24870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24871" type="x-p"/> Reddere quae ferrum valet, exors ipsa secandi. <div eID="gen24871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24872" type="x-p"/> Hor. Ars. Poet., ver. 304. "But let me sharpen others, as the hone <div eID="gen24872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24873" type="x-p"/> Gives edge to razors, though itself have none." <div eID="gen24873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24874" type="x-p"/> Francis.
entries.2eb5793aa30e43d2adebbcada0b564ada0ccc262: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen24874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24875" type="x-p"/> As in water face answereth to face - All men's hearts are pretty nearly alike; water is not more like to water, than one heart is to another. Or, as a man sees his face perfectly reflected by the water, when looking into it; so the wise and penetrating man sees generally what is in the heart of another by considering the general tenor of his words and actions. "Surely, if each man saw another's heart <div eID="gen24875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24876" type="x-p"/> There would be no commerce;All would disperse,And live apart." <div eID="gen24876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24877" type="x-p"/> Hebert.
entries.75bc63d8e31b39808cafebe1eef38eafb8c34c64: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen24877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24878" type="x-p"/> Hell and destruction are never full - How hideous must the soul of a covetous man be, when God compares it to hell and perdition! <div eID="gen24878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24879" type="x-p"/> The eyes of man are never satisfied - As the grave can never be filled up with bodies, nor perdition with souls; so the restless desire, the lust of power, riches, and splendor, is never satisfied. Out of this ever unsatisfied desire spring all the changing fashions, the varied amusements, and the endless modes of getting money, prevalent in every age, and in every country.
entries.280cb409510b3fa13907b863f778ac58507fa0b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen24879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24880" type="x-p"/> As the fining pot for silver - As silver and gold are tried by the art of the refiner, so is a man's heart by the praise he receives. If he feel it not, he deserves it; if he be puffed up by it, he is worthless.
entries.0f46f34e72a0aa621f4a82f2e4ff7534bb966315: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen24880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24881" type="x-p"/> Though thou shouldest bray a fool - Leaving all other conjectures, of which commentators are full, I would propose, that this is a metaphor taken from pounding metallic ores in very large mortars, such as are still common in the East, in order that, when subjected to the action of the fire, the metal may be the more easily separated from the ore. However you may try, by precept or example, or both, to instruct a stupid man, your labor is lost; his foolishness cannot be separated from him. You may purge metals of all their dross; but you cannot purge the fool of his folly.
entries.27bd562c71308f3e07b4d3a109dd07b086859823: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen24881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24882" type="x-p"/> The state of thy flocks - The directions to the end of the chapter refer chiefly to pastoral and agricultural affairs. Do not trust thy flocks to the shepherd merely; number them thyself; look into their condition; see how they are tended; and when, and with what, and in what proportion, they are fed.
entries.480bd8753009b8d48b224e39f6ecc46458420def: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen24882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24883" type="x-p"/> For riches are not for ever - All other kinds of property are very transitory. Money and the highest civil honors are but for a short season. Flocks and herds, properly attended to, may be multiplied and continued from generation to generation. The crown itself is not naturally so permanent.
entries.98ec46ecc6fbd39199f6dba5abb9843219e14b20: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen24883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24884" type="x-p"/> The hay appeareth - Take care that this be timeously mown, carefully dried and safely ricked or housed. And when the tender grass and the proper herbs appear in the mountains in the spring, then send forth the lambs, the young of the flock, that they may get suitable pasturage, without too much impoverishing the home fields; for by the sale of the lambs and goats, the price of the field is paid - all the landlord's demands are discharged. Either a certain number of lambs, goats, and other cattle, was given to the landlord; or so much money as so many lambs, etc., were then worth.
entries.fa9ffb74d0ce89f833b8c74b340729a8e1684c5d: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen24884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24885" type="x-p"/> The lambs are for thy clothing - So many fleeces are given in some places as rent to the landlord.
entries.0c47c4785b2094c7571c9c324c9a651df3edec62: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen24885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24886" type="x-p"/> Goats' milk enough for thy food - ללחמך lelachmecha, "to thy bread;" for they ate the bread and supped the milk to assist mastication, and help deglutition. And it seems that bread, with goats' milk, was the general article of food for the master and his family; and for the servant maids who assisted in the household work, and performed the operations required in the dairy. <div eID="gen24886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24887" type="x-p"/> The reader who wishes to see these maxims detailed and illustrated at large, may consult the writers De Re Rustica, where he will find much curious information.  <chapter eID="Prov.27"/> <div eID="gen24887" type="x-p"/>

entries.9f897b1665ae7105475317625bcf4ca73b64e1fe: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.1">Pro 27:1</reference> <div eID="gen11743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11744" type="x-p"/> In the group <reference osisRef="Prov.27.1-Prov.27.6">Pro 27:1-6</reference> of this chapter every two proverbs form a pair. The first pair is directed against unseemly boasting: 1 Boast not thyself of to-morrow,    For thou knowest not what a day bringeth forth. <div eID="gen11744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11745" type="x-p"/> The ב of בּיום is like, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, that in <reference osisRef="Prov.25.14">Pro 25:14</reference>, the ב of the ground of boasting. One boasts of to-morrow when he boasts of that which he will then do and experience. This boasting is foolish and presumptuous (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.20">Luk 12:20</reference>), for the future is God's; not a moment of the future is in our own power, we know not what a day, this present day or to-morrow (Jam 4:13), will bring forth, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, (cf. Zep 2:2) will disclose, and cannot therefore order anything beforehand regarding it. Instead of לא־תדע (with <hi type="italic">Kametz</hi> and <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>), אל־תדע (thus <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, the Cod. <hi type="italic">Jaman</hi>) is to be written; the Masora knows nothing of that pausal form. And instead of מה־יּלד יום, we write מה יּלד יום with <hi type="italic">Zinnorith</hi>. יּלד before יום has the tone thrown back on the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>., and consequently a shortened ult.; the Masora reckons this word among the twenty-five words with only one <hi type="italic">Tsere</hi>.
entries.0549856b98c37075c6485a610d6285ab53cd7096: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.2">Pro 27:2</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.27.2">2</reference> Let another praise thee, and not thine own mouth;    A stranger, and not thine own lips. <div eID="gen11745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11746" type="x-p"/> The negative לא is with פיך, as in (Arab.) ghyra fyk, bound into one compact idea: that which is not thine own mouth (Fleischer), “not thine own lips,” on the other hand, is not to be interpreted as corresponding to it, like אל־מות, <reference osisRef="Prov.12.28">Pro 12:28</reference>; since after the prohibitive אל, יהללוּך [praise thee] easily supplies itself. זר is properly the stranger, as having come from a distance, and נכרי he who comes from an unknown country, and is himself unknown (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Prov.26.24">Pro 26:24</reference>); the idea of both words, however, passes from <hi type="italic">advena</hi> and <hi type="italic">alienigena</hi> to <hi type="italic">alius</hi>. There is certainly in rare cases a praising of oneself, which is authorized because it is demanded (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.18">2Co 11:18</reference>), which, because it is offered strongly against one’s will, will be measured by truth (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.13">Pro 10:13</reference>); but in general it is improper to applaud oneself, because it is a vain looking at oneself in a glass; it is indecent, because it places others in the shade; imprudent, because it is of no use to us, but only injures, for <hi type="italic">propria laus sordet</hi>, and as Stobäus says, οὐδὲν οὕτως ἄκουσμα φορτικὸν ὡς καθ ̓ αὑτοῦ ἔταινος. Compare the German proverb, “<hi type="italic">Eigenlob stinkt, Freundes Lob hinkt, fremdes Lob klingt</hi>” [= self-praise stinks, a friend’s praise is lame, a stranger’s praise sounds].
entries.4e3ad07437b572c66f37c354ee7351efa1c858aa: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.3">Pro 27:3</reference> <div eID="gen11746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11747" type="x-p"/> The second pair of proverbs designates two kinds of violent passion as unbearable: 3 The heaviness of a stone, the weight of sand -    A fool’s wrath is heavier than both. <div eID="gen11747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11748" type="x-p"/> We do not translate: <hi type="italic">Gravis est petra et onerosa arena</hi>, so that the substantives stand for strengthening the idea, instead of the corresponding adjective (Fleischer, as the lxx, Jerome, Syr., Targum); the two pairs of words stand, as 4a, in genit. relation (cf. on the contrary, <reference osisRef="Prov.31.30">Pro 31:30</reference>), and it is as if the poet said: represent to thyself the heaviness of a stone and the weight of sand, and thou shalt find that the wrath of a fool compared thereto is still heavier, viz., for him who has to bear it; thus heavier, not for the fool himself (Hitzig, Zöckler, Dächsel), but for others against whom his anger goes forth. A Jewish proverb (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Tendlau, No. 901) says, that one knows a man by his wine-glass (כוס), his purse (כיס), and his anger (כעס), viz., how he deports himself in the tumult; and another says that one reads what is in a man ביום כעסו, when he is in an ill-humour. Thus also כעס is to be here understood: the fool in a state of angry, wrathful excitement is so far not master of himself that the worst is to be feared; he sulks and shows hatred, and rages without being appeased; no one can calculate what he may attempt, his behaviour is unendurable. Sand, חול,<note placement="foot">Sand is called by the name חוּל (חיל), to change, whirl, particularly to form sand-wreaths, whence (Arab.) al-Habil, the region of moving sand; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Wetzstein’s <hi type="italic">Nord-arabien</hi>, p. 56.</note> as it appears, as to the number of its grains innumerable, so as to its mass (in weight) immeasurable, <reference osisRef="Job.6.3">Job 6:3</reference>; Sir. 22:13. נטל the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. translates, with strict regard to the etymology, by ἅρμα.
entries.76d12cdb38b11b99e54f3cc681e76a490091ae67: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.4">Pro 27:4</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.27.4">4</reference> The madness of anger, and the overflowing of wrath -    And before jealousy who keeps his place! <div eID="gen11748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11749" type="x-p"/> Here also the two pairs of words 4a stand in connection; אכזריּוּת (for which the Cod. <hi type="italic">Jaman</hi> has incorrectly אכזריות) is the connecting form; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding אכזרי, Pro 5:9. Let one imagine the blind, relentless rage of extreme excitement and irritation, a boiling over of anger like a water-flood, which bears everything down along with it - these paroxysms of wrath do not usually continue long, and it is possible to appease them; but jealousy is a passion that not only rages, but reckons calmly; it incessantly ferments through the mind, and when it breaks forth, he perishes irretrievably who is its object. Fleischer generalizes this idea: “enmity proceeding from hatred, envy, or jealousy, it is difficult or altogether impossible to withstand, since it puts into operation all means, both secretly and openly, to injure the enemy.” But after Pro 6:34., cf. Sol 8:8, there is particularly meant the passion of scorned, mortified, deceived love, viz., in the relation of husband and wife.
entries.4b373182874dc24f4481f020132c34cc96408d3e: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.5">Pro 27:5</reference> <div eID="gen11749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11750" type="x-p"/> The third pair of proverbs passes over from this special love between husband and wife to that subsisting between friends: 5 Better is open accusation    Than secret love. <div eID="gen11750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11751" type="x-p"/> An integral distich; meeאהבה has <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, and instead of the second <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> <hi type="italic">Tarcha</hi>, after <hi type="italic">Thorath Emeth</hi>, p. 11. Zöckler, with Hitzig, incorrectly: better than love which, from false indulgence, keeps concealed from his neighbour his faults, when he ought to tell him of them. That would require the phrase אהבה מסתּרת, not מסתּרת. Dächsel, in order to accommodate the text to this meaning, remarks: concealed censure is concealed love; but it is much rather the neglected duty of love - love without mutual discipline is weak, faint-hearted, and, if it is not too blind to remark in a friend what is worthy of blame, is altogether too forbearing, and essentially without conscience; but it is not “hidden and concealed love.” The meaning of the proverb is different: it is better to be courageously and sternly corrected - on account of some fault committed - by any one, whether he be a foe or a friend, than to be the object of a love which may exist indeed in the heart, but which fails to make itself manifest in outward act. There are men who continually assure us of the reality and depth of their friendship; but when it is necessary for them to prove their love to be self-denying and generous, they are like a torrent which is dry when one expects to drink water from it (<reference osisRef="Job.6.15">Job 6:15</reference>). Such “secret” love, or, since the word is not נסתּרת, but מסתּרת, love confined to the heart alone, is like a fire which, when it burns secretly, neither lightens nor warms; and before such a friend, any one who frankly and freely tells the truth has by far the preference, for although he may pain us, yet he does us good; while the former deceives us, for he leaves us in the lurch when it is necessary to love us, not merely in word and with the tongue, but in deed and in truth (1Jo 3:18). Rightly Fleischer: <hi type="italic">Praestat correptio aperta amicitiae tectae</hi>, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, <hi type="italic">nulla re probatae</hi>.
entries.d4498c9dbc9b13ae110abdf5d7b69083ed742c95: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.6">Pro 27:6</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.27.6">6</reference> Faithful are the wounds of a friend,    And overloaded [plentiful] the kisses of an enemy. <div eID="gen11751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11752" type="x-p"/> The contrast to נאמנים, true, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, honourable and good (with the transference of the character of the person to his act), would be <hi type="italic">fraudulenta</hi> (Jerome), or נהפכות, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, false (Ralbag); Ewald seeks this idea from עתר, to stumble, make a false step;<note placement="foot">Thus also Schultens in the <hi type="italic">Animadversiones</hi>, which later he fancied was derived from עתר, <hi type="italic">nidor</hi>, from the meaning <hi type="italic">nidorosa</hi>, and thence <hi type="italic">virulenta</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen11752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11753" type="x-p"/> Hitzig, from עתר = (Arab.) dadhr, whence dâdhir, <hi type="italic">perfidus</hi>, to gain from; but (1) the comparison does not lie near, since usually the Arab. t corresponds to the Heb. שׁ, and the Arab. d to the Heb. ז; (2) the Heb. עתר has already three meanings, and it is not advisable to load it with yet another meaning assumed for this passage, and elsewhere not found. The three meanings are the following: (a) to smoke, Aram. עטר, whence עתר, vapour, <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.11">Eze 8:11</reference>, according to which the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>., with Kimchi’s and Parchon’s <hi type="italic">Lex</hi>., translates: the kisses of an enemy συνωμίχλωνται, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, are fog; (b) to sacrifice, to worship, Arab. atar; according to which Aquila: ἱκετικά (as, with Grabe, it is probably to be read for ἑκούσια of the lxx); and agreeably to the <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>., but too artificially, Arama: obtained by entreaties = constrained; (c) to heap up, whence <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. העתיר, <reference osisRef="Ezek.35.13">Eze 35:13</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.33.6">Jer 33:6</reference>, according to which Rashi, Meîri, Gesenius, Fleischer, Bertheau, and most explain, cogn. with עשׁר, whose Aram. form is עתר, for עשׁר is properly a heap of goods or treasures.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., regarding this word, Schlottmann in <hi type="italic">Deutsch.-Morgenl. Zeitschrift</hi>, xxiv. 665, 668.</note> <div eID="gen11753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11754" type="x-p"/> This third meaning gives to the kisses of an enemy a natural adjective: they are too abundant, so much the more plentiful to veil over the hatred, like the kisses by means of which Judas betrayed his Lord, not merely denoted by φιλεῖν, but by καταφιλεῖν, Mat 26:49. This, then, is the contrast, that the strokes inflicted by one who truly loves us, although they tear into our flesh (פּצע, from פּצע, to split, to tear open), yet are faithful (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.141.5">Psa 141:5</reference>); on the contrary, the enemy covers over with kisses him to whom he wishes all evil. Thus also נעתרות forms an indirect contrast to נאמנים.
entries.b70d36becfabbb74f8a6f2a80f795d9a425dbb05: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.7">Pro 27:7</reference> <div eID="gen11754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11755" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Prov.27.7-Prov.27.10">Pro 27:7-10</reference> there is also visible a weaving of the external with the internal. First, there are two proverbs, in each of which there is repeated a word terminating with נ. 7 A satisfied soul treadeth honeycomb under foot;    And a hungry soul - everything bitter is (to it) sweet. <div eID="gen11755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11756" type="x-p"/> It is unnecessary to read תּבוּז (Hitzig); תּבוּס is stronger; “to tread with the feet” is the extreme degree of scornful despite. That satiety and hunger are applicable to the soul, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Pro 10:3. In 7b, the adverb להּ, relative to the <hi type="italic">nomin</hi>. <hi type="italic">absol</hi>., like <reference osisRef="Prov.28.7">Pro 28:7</reference>, but not Pro 13:18. “Hunger is the best cook,” according to a German proverb; the Hebrew proverb is so formed that it is easily transferred to the sphere of the soul. Let the man whom God has richly satisfied with good things guard himself against ingratitude towards the Giver, and against an undervaluing of the gifts received; and if they are spiritual blessings, let him guard himself against self-satisfaction and self-contentment, which is, in truth, the worst poverty, <reference osisRef="Rev.3.17">Rev 3:17</reference>; for life without God is a constant hunger and thirst. There is in worldly things, even the most pleasing, a dissatisfaction felt, and a dissatisfaction awakening disgust; and in spiritual life, a satiety which supposes itself to be full of life, but which is nothing else than the decay of life, than the changing of life into death.
entries.3cd985bfdb2b31cf12429064e560fd5015c01a63: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.8">Pro 27:8</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.27.8">8</reference> As a bird that wandereth from her nest,    So is a man that wandereth from his home. <div eID="gen11756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11757" type="x-p"/> It is not a flying out that is meant, from which at any moment a return is possible, but an unwilling taking to flight (lxx 8b: ὅταν ἀποξενωθῇ; <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>.: πλανούμενον ... πλανούμενος); for עוף נודד, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.2">Isa 16:2</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.4.25">Jer 4:25</reference>, birds that have been frightened; and נדד, Pro 21:15., designates the fugitive; cf. נע ונד, <reference osisRef="Gen.4.14">Gen 4:14</reference>, and above, <reference osisRef="Prov.26.2">Pro 26:2</reference>, where נוּד designates aimless roving about. Otherwise Fleischer: “warning against unnecessary roaming about, in journeyings and wanderings far from home: as a bird far from its nest is easily wounded, caught, or killed, so, on such excursions, one easily comes to injury and want. One may think of a journey in the East. The Arabs say, in one of their proverbs: âlsafar ḳaṭ'at man âlklyym (= journeying is a part of the pains of hell).” But נדד here is not to be understood in the sense of a <hi type="italic">libere vagari</hi>. Rightly C. B. Michaelis: <hi type="italic">qui vagatur extorris et exul a loco suo sc. natali vel habitationis ordinariae</hi>. This proverb mediately recommends the love of one’s fatherland, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, “love to the land in which our father has his home; on which our paternal mansion stands; in which we have spent the years of our childhood, so significant a part of one’s whole life; from which we have derived our bodily and intellectual nourishment; and in which home we recognise bone of our bone and flesh of our flesh.”<note placement="foot">Gustave Baur’s article “Vaterlandsliebe,” in Schmid’s <hi type="italic">Pädagogischer Encyklopädie</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen11757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11758" type="x-p"/> But next it says, that to be in a strange land must be an unhappiness, because a man never feels better than at home, as the bird in its nest. We say: <hi type="italic">Heimat</hi> [home] - this beautiful word becomes the German language, which has also coined the expressive idea of <hi type="italic">Heimweh</hi> [longing for home]; the Heb. uses, to express the idea of home, the word מקומי; and of fatherland, the word ארצי or אדמתי. The Heb. שׁבוּת corresponds<note placement="foot">The translators transfer to this place a note from vol. ii. p. 191f. of the author’s larger <hi type="italic">Comm. ü. den Psalter</hi>, to which Delitzsch refers the reader: - “The modern High German adj. <hi type="italic">elend</hi>, middle High German <hi type="italic">ellende</hi>, old High German <hi type="italic">alilandi, elilendi</hi>, or <hi type="italic">elilenti</hi>, is composed of <hi type="italic">ali</hi> and <hi type="italic">land</hi>. The adj. <hi type="italic">ali</hi> occurs only in old High German in composition. In the Gothic it is found as an independent adj., in the sense of <hi type="italic">alius</hi> and ἄλλυς (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Ulfilas, <reference osisRef="Gal.5.10">Gal 5:10</reference></note>. The primary meaning of <hi type="italic">elilenti</hi> is consequently: of another country, foreign. In glosses and translations it is rendered by the Lat. words <hi type="italic">peregrinus, exul, advena</hi>, also <hi type="italic">captivus</hi>. In these meanings it occurs very frequently. In the old High German translation of Ammonius, <hi type="italic">Diatessaron</hi>, <hi type="italic">sive Harmoniae in quatuor Evangelica</hi>, the word proselytism, occurring in <reference osisRef="Matt.23.15">Mat 23:15</reference>, is rendered by <hi type="italic">elilantan</hi>. To the adj. the old High German subst. corresponds. This has the meaning <hi type="italic">exilium, transmigratio, captivitas</hi>. The connection in <hi type="italic">elilenti</hi> or <hi type="italic">elilentes</hi>, used adverbially, is rendered by the Lat. <hi type="italic">peregre</hi>. In the middle High German, however, the proper signification of both words greatly predominates. But as, in the old High German, the idea of <hi type="italic">miser</hi> is often at the same time comprehended in the proper signification: he who is miserable through banishment, imprisonment, or through sojourning in a strange land; thus, in several places of the middle High German, this derived idea begins to separate itself from the fundamental conception, so that <hi type="italic">ellende</hi> comes in general to be called <hi type="italic">miser</hi>. In the new High German this derived conception is almost alone maintained. Yet here also, in certain connections, there are found traces of the original idea, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <hi type="italic">in’s Elend schicken</hi>, for to banish. Very early also the word came to be used, in a spiritual sense, to denote our present abode, in contrast to paradise or the heavenly kingdom.... Thus, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, in one of Luther’s hymns, when we pray to the Holy Ghost: <div eID="gen11758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11759" type="x-p"/> Das er vns behüte, an vnserm ende, <div eID="gen11759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11760" type="x-p"/> Wenn wir heim farn aus diesem elende.” [That He guard us to our end <div eID="gen11760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11761" type="x-p"/> When we go home from this world.]  - Rud. von Raumer) to the German <hi type="italic">Elend</hi>, but = <hi type="italic">Ellend, elilenti</hi>, of another land, strange.
entries.775f8c8092c51678632f60b92b34d4e8b85af545: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.9">Pro 27:9</reference> <div eID="gen11761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11762" type="x-p"/> The two following proverbs have in common the catchword רע, and treat of the value of friendship: - 9 Oil and frankincense rejoice the heart;    And the sweet discourse of a friend from a counselling of soul. <div eID="gen11762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11763" type="x-p"/> Regarding the perfuming with dry aromas, and sprinkling with liquid aromas, as a mark of honour towards guests, and as a means of promoting joyful social fellowship, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 7:16., Pro 21:17. The pred. ישׂמּח comprehends frankincense or oil as the two sides of one and the same thing; the lxx introduces, from <reference osisRef="Ps.104.15">Psa 104:15</reference>, also wine. It also reads ומתק רעה as one word, וּמתקרעת: καταῤῥήγνυται δὲ ὑπὸ συμπτωμάτων ψυχή, which Hitzig regards as original; for he translates, understanding מעצת after <reference osisRef="Ps.13.3">Psa 13:3</reference>, “but the soul is torn by cares.” But why מתקרעה, this <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. without example, for נקרעה? and now connected with מן in the sense of ὑπό! And what does one gain by this Alexandrian wisdom [of the lxx] - a contrast to 9a which is altogether incongruous? Döderlein’s rendering accords far better with 9a: “but the sweetness of a friend surpasses fragrant wood.” But although this rendering of the word [עצה] by “fragrant wood” is found in Gesen. <hi type="italic">Lex</hi>., from one edition to another, yet it must be rejected; for the word signifies wood as the contents of trees, the word for aromatic wood must be עצים; and if the poet had not intentionally aimed at dubiety, he ought to have written עצי בשׂם, since נפשׁ, which the exception of <reference osisRef="Isa.3.20">Isa 3:20</reference>, where it is beyond doubt, nowhere means fragrance. If we read עצת and נפשׁ together, then we may suppose that the latter designates the soul, as at <reference osisRef="Ps.13.3">Psa 13:3</reference>; and the former, counsel (from the verb יעץ). But to what does the suffix of רעהוּ refer? One may almost conjecture that the words originally were וּמתק נפשׁ מעצת רעהוּ, and the sweetness of the soul (<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, a sweet relish for it, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.27.7">Pro 27:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.16.24">Pro 16:24</reference>) consists in the counsel of a friend, according to which Jerome translates: <hi type="italic">et bonis amici conciliis anima dulcoratur</hi>. By this transposition רעהו refers back to נפשׁ; for is nephesh denote a person or a living being, it can be construed <hi type="italic">ad sensum</hi> as masc., <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Num 31:28. But the words may remain in the order in which they are transmitted to us. It is possible that רעהוּ is (Böttcher refers to <reference osisRef="Job.12.4">Job 12:4</reference>) of the same meaning as הרע (the friend of one = the friend), as כלּו denotes directly the whole; חציו, the half; עתּו, the right time. Recognising this, Cocceius, Umbreit, Stier, and Zöckler explain: sweetness, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the sweet encouragement (מתק, in the sense of “sweetness (grace) of the lips,” <reference osisRef="Prov.16.21">Pro 16:21</reference>) of a friend, is better than one’s own counsel, than prudence seeking to help oneself, and trusting merely to one’s own resources; thus also Rashi: better than what one’s own soul advises him. But (1) נפשׁ cannot mean one’s own person (oneself) in contrast to another person; and (2) this does not supply a correct antithesis to 9a. Thus מן will not express the preference, but the origin. Accordingly Ewald, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, explains: the sweetness of a friend whom one has proceedeth from the counsel of soul, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, from such counsel as is drawn from a deep, full soul. But no proof can be brought from the usage of the language that עצת־נפשׁ can be so meant; these words, after the analogy of דעת נפשׁ, <reference osisRef="Prov.19.2">Pro 19:2</reference>, mean ability to give counsel as a quality of the soul (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.14">Pro 8:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.12.13">Pro 12:13</reference>), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, its ability to advise. Accordingly, with Bertheau, we explain ישׂמח־לב as the common predicate for 9a and 9b: ointment and perfume rejoice the heart, and (The Syr., Targ., well: even so) the sweet exhortation of a friend, from a soul capable of rendering counsel; also, this and this, more than that fragrance. This proverb is formed in the same way as <reference osisRef="Prov.26.9">Pro 26:9</reference>, Pro 26:14. In this explanation רעהו is well referred back to לב: and (more than) the sweet advice of his friend. But not so that רעהו is equivalent to רע הלּב, for one does not thus speak; but the construction is as when we say, in the German language: <hi type="italic">Nichts thut einem Herzen woler als wenn sein Freund es mitfühlend tröstet</hi> [nothing does more good to a heart than when a friend sympathizingly comforts it]; or: <hi type="italic">Zage nicht, tief betrübtes Herz! Dein Freund lebt und wird dir bald sich zeigen</hi> [Be not dismayed, deeply-troubled heart! thy friend lives, and will soon show himself to thee]. In such cases the word “<hi type="italic">Herz</hi>” [heart] does not designate a distinct part of the person, but, synecdochically, it denotes the whole person.
entries.5d117f46bb96ea0570787f0d4390dc456e104d17: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.10">Pro 27:10</reference> <div eID="gen11763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11764" type="x-p"/> Another proverb, consisting of three lines, in commendation of friendship: <div eID="gen11764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11765" type="x-p"/> Thine own friend and the friend of thy father forsake not, <div eID="gen11765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11766" type="x-p"/> And into thy brother’s house go not in the day of thy misfortune - <div eID="gen11766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11767" type="x-p"/> Better is a near neighbour than a far-off brother. <div eID="gen11767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11768" type="x-p"/> In our editions רעך is incorrectly appointed with <hi type="italic">Pasek</hi> after it, so that the accent is <hi type="italic">Asla Legarmeh</hi>; the <hi type="italic">Pasek</hi> is, after the example of older editions, with Norzi, to be cancelled, so that only the conjunctive <hi type="italic">Asla</hi> remains; “thine own and the friend of thy father” denotes the family friend, like some family heirloom, descending from father to son. Such an old tried friend one must certainly not give up. The Kerı̂ changes the second ורעה into ורע, but ורעה (which, after the Masora in <hi type="italic">st. constr</hi>., retains its <hi type="italic">segol</hi>, Ewald, §211e) is also admissible, for a form of comparison (Hitzig) this רעה is not, but the fuller form of the abbreviated רע, from רעה, to take care of, to tend, to pasture - an infinitive formation (= רעי) like the Arab. cogn. râ'in a participial.
