Such a proved friend one ought certainly not to give up, and in the time of heavy trial (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding איד, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.26">Pro 1:26</reference>) one should go to him and not to a brother’s house - it is by this supposed that, as <reference osisRef="Prov.18.24">Pro 18:24</reference> says, there is a degree of friendship (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.17.17">Pro 17:17</reference>) which in regard to attachment stands above that of mere fraternal relationship, and it is true; blood-relationship, viewed in itself, stands as a relationship of affection on natural grounds below friendship, which is a relationship of life on moral grounds. But does blood-relationship exclude friendship of soul? cannot my brother be at the same time my heart-friend? and is not friendship all the firmer when it has at the same time its roots in the spirit and in natural grounds? The poet seems to have said this, for in 10c, probably a popular saying (cf. “<hi type="italic">Besser Nachbar an der Wand als Bruder über Land</hi>” [Better a neighbour by one’s side than a brother abroad]), he gives to his advice a foundation, and at the same time a limitation which modifies its ruggedness. But Dächsel places (like Schultens) in קרוב and רחוק meanings which the words do not contain, for he interprets them of inward nearness and remoteness; and Zöckler reads between the lines, for he remarks, a “near neighbour” is one who is near to the oppressed to counsel and help them, and a “distant brother” is one who with an unamiable disposition remains far from the oppressed. The state of the matter is simple. If one has a tried friend in neighbourly nearness, so in the time of distress, when he needs consolation and help, he must go to this friend, and not first to the house of a brother dwelling at a distance, for the former certainly does for us what the latter probably may and probably may not do for us.
entries.282458aedb9f9c7646f9c5a8d4391b6168f331cd: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.11">Pro 27:11</reference> <div eID="gen11768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11769" type="x-p"/> This proverb has, in common with the preceding tristich, the form of an address: <div eID="gen11769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11770" type="x-p"/> Become wise, my son, and make my heart rejoice, <div eID="gen11770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11771" type="x-p"/> That I may give an answer to my accusers. <div eID="gen11771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11772" type="x-p"/> Better than “be wise” (Luther), we translate “become wise” (lxx σοφὸς γίνου); for he who is addressed might indeed be wise, though not at present so, so that his father is made to listen to such deeply wounding words as these, “Cursed be he who begat, and who educated this man” (Malbim). The cohortative clause 11b (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.119.42">Psa 119:42</reference>) has the force of a clause with a purpose (Gesen. §128:1): <hi type="italic">ut habeam quod iis qui me convicientur regerere possim</hi>; it does not occur anywhere in the Hezekiah collection except here.
entries.5475100c6d80080f3922b35effde09f72a4a7537: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.12">Pro 27:12</reference>     ערום appears to lean on חכם. <div eID="gen11772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11773" type="x-p"/> The prudent man seeth the misfortune, hideth himself; <div eID="gen11773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11774" type="x-p"/> The simple pass on, suffer injury. = <reference osisRef="Prov.22.3">Pro 22:3</reference>, where וּפתיים for פּתאים, ונסתּר for נסתּר, and ונענשׁוּ for נענשׁוּ; the three <hi type="italic">asyndeta</hi> make the proverb clumsy, as if it counted out its seven words separately to the hearer. Ewald, §349a, calls it a “<hi type="italic">Steinschrift</hi>” an inscription on a stone. The perfects united in pairs with, and yet more without, <hi type="italic">Vav</hi>, express the coincidence<note placement="foot">The second <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> is at <reference osisRef="Prov.22.3">Pro 22:3</reference>, as well as here, according to the rule <reference osisRef="Prov.18.4">Pro 18:4</reference> of the <hi type="italic">Accentuationssystem</hi>, the transformation of the <hi type="italic">Dechi</hi>, and preserves its value of interpunction; the <hi type="italic">Legarmeh</hi> of ערום is, however, a disjunctive of less force than <hi type="italic">Dechi</hi>, so that thus the sequence of the accents denotes that ערום ראה רעה is a clause related to ונסתר as a hypothetical antecedent: if the prudent sees the calamity, then he hides himself from it. This syntactic relation is tenable at <reference osisRef="Prov.22.3">Pro 22:3</reference>, but not here at Pro 27:12. Here, at least, ערום would be better with <hi type="italic">Rebia</hi>, to which the following <hi type="italic">Dechi</hi> would subordinate itself. The prudent seeth the evil, concealeth himself; or also, prudent is he who sees the evil, hides himself. For of two disjunctives before <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi>, the first, according as it is greater or less than the second, retains either <hi type="italic">Legarmeh</hi> (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.1.5">Psa 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.86.12">Psa 86:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.14">Psa 88:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.109.14">Psa 109:14</reference>) or <hi type="italic">Rebia</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.12.2">Pro 12:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.2">Psa 25:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.9">Psa 69:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.146.5">Psa 146:5</reference>).</note> as to time.
entries.06d194ea66806e4ba15aafdc47dca83d5f3e892a: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.13">Pro 27:13</reference>     ערום alliterates with ערב. <div eID="gen11774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11775" type="x-p"/> Take from him the garment, for he hath become surety for another, <div eID="gen11775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11776" type="x-p"/> And for the sake of a strange matter put him under bonds. = <reference osisRef="Prov.20.16">Pro 20:16</reference>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., there. נכריּה we interpret neut. (lxx τὰ ἀλλότρια; Jerome, <hi type="italic">pro alienis</hi>), although certainly the case occurs that one becomes surety for a strange woman (Aquila, Theodotion, περὶ ξένης), by whose enticements and flatteries he is taken, and who afterwards leaves him in the lurch with the debts for which he had become security, to show her costly favour to another.
entries.db1d9cab42886af56469a84cf6b9aced66958156: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.14">Pro 27:14</reference> <div eID="gen11776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11777" type="x-p"/> This proverb, passing over the three immediately intervening, connects itself with <reference osisRef="Prov.27.9">Pro 27:9</reference> and Pro 27:10. It is directed against cringing, noisy complimenting: <div eID="gen11777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11778" type="x-p"/> He who blesseth his neighbour with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, <div eID="gen11778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11779" type="x-p"/> It is reckoned as a curse to him. <div eID="gen11779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11780" type="x-p"/> The first line is intentionally very heavy, in order to portray the empressement of the maker of compliments: he calls out to another his good wishes with a loud voice, so as to make the impression of deep veneration, of deeply felt thankfulness, but in reality to gain favour thereby, and to commend himself to greater acts of kindness; he sets himself to meet him, having risen up (השׁכּים, adverbial <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. <hi type="italic">abs</hi>.; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.44.4">Jer 44:4</reference> with <reference osisRef="Jer.25.4">Jer 25:4</reference>) early in the morning, to offer his <hi type="italic">captatio benevolentiae</hi> as speedily as possible; but this salutation of good wishes, the affected zeal in presenting which is a sign of a selfish, calculating, servile soul, is reckoned to him as קללה, viz., before God and every one who can judge correctly of human nature, also before him who is complimented in so ostentatious and troublesome a manner, the true design of which is thus seen. Others understand the proverb after the example of <hi type="italic">Berachoth</hi> 14a, that one ought to salute no one till he has said his morning’s prayer, because honour is due before all to God (the Book of Wisdom, 10:28); and others after <hi type="italic">Erachin</hi> 16a, according to which one is meant who was invited as a guest of a generous lord, and was liberally entertained, and who now on the public streets blesses him, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, praises him for his nobility of mind - such blessing is a curse to him whom it concerns, because this trumpeting of his praise brings upon him a troublesome, importunate crowd. But plainly the particularity of 'בּקול וגו lays the chief emphasis on the servility manifested; and one calls to mind the case of the clients besieging the doors of their patrons, those <hi type="italic">clientes matutini</hi>, each of whom sought to be the first in the <hi type="italic">salutatio</hi> of his distinguished wealthy patron.
entries.2e1d86756ae96138e0d12fc461e0c01dae55c678: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.15">Pro 27:15</reference> <div eID="gen11780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11781" type="x-p"/> This proverb passes from the <hi type="italic">complimentarius</hi> to its opposite, a shrewish wife: <div eID="gen11781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11782" type="x-p"/> A continual dropping in a rainy day <div eID="gen11782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11783" type="x-p"/> And a contentious woman are alike. <div eID="gen11783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11784" type="x-p"/> Thus we have already translated (vol. i. p. 9), where, when treating of the manifold forms of parabolic proverbs, we began with this least poetic, but at the same time remarked that <reference osisRef="Prov.27.15">Pro 27:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.27.16">Pro 27:16</reference> are connected, forming a tetrastich, which is certainly the case according to the text here lying before us. In <reference osisRef="Prov.27.15">Pro 27:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.19.13">Pro 19:13</reference> is expanded into a distich, and made a complete verse. Regarding דּלף טורד, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., the explanation there given. The noun סגריר, which the Syr. translates by magyaa', but the Targumist retains, because it is in common use in the post-bibl. Heb. (<hi type="italic">Bereschith rabba</hi>, c. 1) and the Jewish Aramaic, signifies violent rain, after the Jewish interpreters, because then the people remain shut up in their houses; more correctly, perhaps, from the unbroken continuousness and thickness (cf. the Arab. insajara, to go behind each other in close column) with which the rain pours down. Regarding מדונים, Kerı̂ מדינים, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.6.14">Pro 6:14</reference>; the genit. connection of 'אושׁת מ we have already at Pro 21:9. The form נשׁתּוה is doubtful. If accented, with Löwenstein and others, as <hi type="italic">Milra</hi>, then we would have a <hi type="italic">Nithkatal</hi> before us, as at Num 1:47, or a <hi type="italic">Hothkatal</hi> - a passive form of the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>, the existence of which, however, is not fully established. Rather this word is to be regarded as נשׁתּוּה (<hi type="italic">Nithpa</hi>. as <reference osisRef="Deut.21.8">Deu 21:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.48">Eze 23:48</reference>) without the dagesh, and lengthened; the form of the word נשׁתּוה, as found in the Cod. <hi type="italic">Jaman</hi>., aims at this. But the form נשׁתּוה is better established, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, by Cod. 1294, as <hi type="italic">Milel</hi>. Kimchi, <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 131a (cf. Ewald, §132c), regards it as a form without the <hi type="italic">dagesh</hi>, made up the <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. and <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>., leaving the <hi type="italic">penultima</hi> toning unexplained. Bertheau regards it as a voluntative: let us compare (as נשׁתּעה, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.23">Isa 41:23</reference>); but as he himself says, the reflexive form does not accord with this sense. Hitzig has adopted the right explanation (cf. Olshausen, §275, and Böttcher, §1072, who, however, registers it at random as an Ephraimitism). נשׁתּוה is a <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi>, with a transposition of consonants for נשׁותה, since נשׁותה passes over into נשׁתּוה. Such is now the <hi type="italic">genus</hi> in the arrangement; the <hi type="italic">Milra</hi> form would be as masc. syntactically inaccurate. “The finite following the subjects is regulated by the gender and number of that which is next before it, as at <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.22">2Sa 3:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.20">2Sa 20:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.6">Psa 55:6</reference>; Job 19:15” (Hitzig).
entries.5b98f728faddca445d275ff42f34ba2f7ad8ca68: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.16">Pro 27:16</reference> <div eID="gen11784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11785" type="x-p"/> This verse stands in close connection with the preceding, for it speaks of the contentious woman: <div eID="gen11785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11786" type="x-p"/> He that restraineth her restraineth the wind, <div eID="gen11786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11787" type="x-p"/> And oil meeteth his right hand. <div eID="gen11787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11788" type="x-p"/> The connection of the plur. subject צפניה = <hi type="italic">quicunque eam cohibet</hi>, with a sing. predicate, is not to be disputed (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.3.18">Pro 3:18</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.28.16">Pro 28:16</reference>, Chethı̂b); but can צפן gain from the meaning of preserving, laying up, also the meanings of keeping, of confining, and shutting up? - for these meanings we have כּלא and עצר (cf. צרר, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.4">Pro 30:4</reference>). In 16b it lies nearer to see in ימינו the object of the clause (oil meeteth his right hand) than the subject (his right hand meeteth oil), for the gender of ימין directs to יד (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.15.6">Eze 15:6</reference>; cf. 6a, where נאדּרי is as to gender indifferent): it is fem., while on the contrary שׁמן is generally masc. (cf. Sol 1:3). There is no reason for regarding ימינו as an adverbial accus. (he meets oil with his right hand), or, with Hitzig, as a second subject (he meets oil, his right hand); the latter, in the order of the words lying before us, is not at all possible. We suppose that יקרא, as at <reference osisRef="Gen.49.1">Gen 49:1</reference>, is equivalent to יקרה (Ewald, §116c), for the explanation <hi type="italic">oleum dexterae ejus praeconem agit</hi> (Cocceius, Schultens) does not explain, but only darkens: and <hi type="italic">oleum dexterâ suâ legit</hi>, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, colligit (Fleischer), is based on an untenable use of the word. As one may say of person to person, קרך, <hi type="italic">occurrit tibi</hi>, Num 25:18, so also יקרא (יקרה), of a thing that meets a man or one of his members; and if we compare לקראת and קרי, then for 16b the meaning is possible: oil meets his right hand; the quarrelsome woman is like oil that cannot be held in the hand, which struggles against that which holds it, for it always glides out of the hand. Thus also Luther: “and seeks to hold oil with his hand,” as if he read יקמץ. In fact, this word was more commonly used as the expression of untenableness than the colourless and singular word יקרא, which, besides, is so ambiguous, that none of the old translators has thought on any other קרא than that which signifies “to call,” “to name.” The Jewish interpreters also adhere to this nearest lying קרא, and, moreover, explain, as the Syr., Targ., Aquila, Symmachus, Jerome, and the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>., שׁמן ימינו, according to the accentuation as genit. connected, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Rashi: he calls for oil to his right hand, viz., as the means of purification from leprosy, <reference osisRef="Lev.8.14">Lev 8:14</reference> [Lev 14:16]; and Aben Ezra: even when he calls for oil to his right hand, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, would move them to silence with the precious anointing oil. Perhaps <reference osisRef="Prov.27.16">Pro 27:16</reference> was originally an independent proverb as follows: צפני הון צפן רוח ושמן ימינו יקרא <div eID="gen11788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11789" type="x-p"/> He who layeth up riches in store layeth up the wind, <div eID="gen11789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11790" type="x-p"/> And he nameth them the fat of his right hand;<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, he sees in them that which makes his right hand fat and strong (שׁמן, as at <reference osisRef="Ps.109.24">Psa 109:24</reference>, opp. Zec 11:17; cf. בּמשׁמנּיו, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.16">Isa 10:16</reference>, and regarding Ἐσμούν, the Phoenician god of health, at <reference osisRef="Isa.59.10">Isa 59:10</reference>), and yet it is only the wind, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, something that is worthless and transient, which he stored up (צפן, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.13.22">Pro 13:22</reference>, and in מצפּניו, Obad. Oba 1:6). הון is used as it frequently occurs in the Book of Proverbs, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.4">Pro 11:4</reference>, and the whole proverb expresses by another figure the same as Pro 18:11. The fact that צפון (רוח), <reference osisRef="Prov.25.23">Pro 25:23</reference>, and as a contrast thereto in the compass ימין (the south), hovered before the poet, may not have been without its influence on the choice of the words and expression here.
entries.e60cafb66343aef60f9aa17facd0734a9ff65da8: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.17">Pro 27:17</reference> <div eID="gen11790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11791" type="x-p"/> This proverb expresses the influence arising from the intercourse of man with man: <div eID="gen11791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11792" type="x-p"/> Iron is sharpened by iron, <div eID="gen11792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11793" type="x-p"/> And a man may sharpen the appearance of another. <div eID="gen11793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11794" type="x-p"/> When the Masora reads יחד, Ewald remarks, it interprets the word as denoting “at the same time,” and the further meaning of the proverb must then accord therewith. Accordingly he translates: “iron together with iron! and one together with the face of another!” But then the prep. ב or עם is wanting after the second יחד - for יחד is, in spite of Ewald, §217h, never a prep. - and the “face,” 17b, would be a perplexing superfluity. Hitzig already replies, but without doing homage to the traditional text-punctuation, that such a violence to the use of language, and such a darkening of the thought, is not at all to be accepted. He suggests four ways of interpreting יחד: (1) the adverb יחד, united, properly (taken accusat.) union; (2) יחד, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.11">Psa 86:11</reference>, imper. of the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> יחד, unite; (3) יחדּ, <reference osisRef="Job.3.6">Job 3:6</reference>, jussive of the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> חדה, <hi type="italic">gaudeat</hi>; and (4) as Kimchi, in <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 126a, jussive of the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> חדה (= חדד) <hi type="italic">acuere</hi>, after the form תחז, Mic 4:11. ויּחץ, <reference osisRef="Gen.32.8">Gen 32:8</reference>, etc. <hi type="italic">in p</hi>. יחד, after the form אחז, Job 23:9. ויּחל, 2Ki 1:2 (= ויּחלא, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.12">2Ch 16:12</reference>). If we take יחד with בּרזל, then it is <hi type="italic">à priori</hi> to be supposed that in יחד the idea of sharpening lies; in the Arab. iron is simply called hadyda = חדוּד, that which is sharpened, sharp; and a current Arab. proverb says: alḥadyd balḥadyd yuflah = <hi type="italic">ferrum ferro diffinditur</hi> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Freytag under the word falah). But is the traditional text-punctuation thus understood to be rightly maintained? It may be easily changed in conformity with the meaning, but not so that with Böttcher we read יחד and יחד, the <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> of חדד: “iron sharpeneth itself on iron, and a man sharpeneth himself over against his neighbour” - for פני after a verb to be understood actively, has to be regarded as the object - but since יחד is changed into יחד (<hi type="italic">fut</hi>. <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. of חדד), and יחד into יחד or יחד (<hi type="italic">fut</hi>. <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. of חדד, after the form אחל, <hi type="italic">incipiam</hi>, <reference osisRef="Deut.2.25">Deu 2:25</reference>, or אחל, <hi type="italic">profanabo</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.39.7">Eze 39:7</reference>; Num 30:3). The passive rendering of the idea 17a and the active of 17b thus more distinctly appear, and the unsuitable jussive forms are set aside: <hi type="italic">ferrum ferro exacuitur, et homo exacuit faciem amici sui</hi> (Jerome, Targ., the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>.). But that is not necessary. As ויּעל may be the <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. of the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. (he brought up) as well as of the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> (he went up), so יחד may be regarded as <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>, and יחד as <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. Fleischer prefers to render יחד also as <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>.: <hi type="italic">aciem exhibet</hi>, like יעשׁיר, <hi type="italic">divitias acquirit</hi>, and the like; but the jussive is not favourable to this supposition of an intransitive (inwardly transitive) <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. It may indeed be said that the two jussives appear to be used, according to poetic licence, with the force of indicatives (cf. under <reference osisRef="Prov.12.26">Pro 12:26</reference>), but the repetition opposes it. Thus we explain: iron is sharpened [<hi type="italic">gewetzt</hi>, Luther uses this appropriate word] by iron (ב of the means, not of the object, which was rather to be expected in 17b after <reference osisRef="Prov.20.30">Pro 20:30</reference>), and a man whets פני, the appearance, the deportment, the nature, and manner of the conduct of his neighbour. The proverb requires that the intercourse of man with man operate in the way of sharpening the manner and forming the habits and character; that one help another to culture and polish of manner, rub off his ruggedness, round his corners, as one has to make use of iron when he sharpens iron and seeks to make it bright. The jussive form is the oratorical form of the expression of that which is done, but also of that which is to be done.
entries.2a46436f340902bc3c7c8231ce3273b009d10460: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.18">Pro 27:18</reference> <div eID="gen11794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11795" type="x-p"/> The following three proverbs are connected with 17 in their similarity of form: - 18 Whosoever watcheth the fig-tree will enjoy its fruit;      And he that hath regard to his master attaineth to honour. <div eID="gen11795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11796" type="x-p"/> The first member is, as in <reference osisRef="Prov.27.17">Pro 27:17</reference>, only the means of contemplating the second; as faithful care of the tree has fruit for a reward, so faithful regard for one’s master, honour; נצר is used as at <reference osisRef="Isa.27.3">Isa 27:3</reference>, שׁמר as at Hos 4:10, etc. - the proverb is valid in the case of any kind of master up to the Lord of lords. The fig-tree presented itself, as Heidenheim remarks, as an appropriate figure; because in the course of several years’ training it brings forth its fruit, which the language of the Mishna distinguishes as פגין, unripe, בוחל, half ripe, and צמל, fully ripe. To fruit in the first line corresponds honour in the second, which the faithful and attentive servant attains unto first on the part of his master, and then also from society in general.
entries.ed122a65524104ffab6141500eb98eca3964915c: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.19">Pro 27:19</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.27.19">19</reference> As it is with water, face correspondeth to face,      So also the heart of man to man. <div eID="gen11796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11797" type="x-p"/> Thus the traditional text is to be translated; for on the supposition that כּמּים must be used for כּבמּים, yet it might not be translated: as in waters face corresponds to face (Jerome: <hi type="italic">quomodo in aquis resplendent vultus respicientium</hi>), because כּ (<hi type="italic">instar</hi>) is always only a prep. and never conj. subordinating to itself a whole sentence (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Ps.38.14">Psa 38:14</reference>). But whether כּמּים, “like water,” may be an abridgment of a sentence: “like as it is with water,” is a question, and the translation of the lxx (Syr., Targ., Arab.), ὥσπερ οὐχ ὅμοια πρόσωπα προσώποις, κ.τ.λ., appears, according to Böttcher’s ingenious conjecture, to have supposed כאשר במים, from which the lxx derived כּאין דּמים, <hi type="italic">sicut non pares</hi>. The thought is beautiful: as in the water-mirror each one beholds his own face (Luther: <hi type="italic">der Scheme</hi> = the shadow), so out of the heart of another each sees his own heart, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, he finds in another the dispositions and feelings of his own heart (Fleischer) - the face finds in water its reflection, and the heart of a man finds in man its echo; men are ὁμοιοπαθεῖς, and it is a fortunate thing that their heart is capable of the same sympathetic feelings, so that one can pour into the heart of another that which fills and moves his own heart, and can there find agreement with it, and a re-echo. The expression with ל is extensive: one corresponds to another, one belongs to another, is adapted to the other, turns to the other, so that the thought may be rendered in manifold ways: the divinely-ordained mutual relationship is always the ground-thought. This is wholly obliterated by Hitzig’s conjecture כּמוּם, “what a mole on the face is to the face, that is man’s heart to man,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the heart is the dark spot in man, his <hi type="italic">partie honteuse</hi>. But the Scripture nowhere speaks of the human heart after this manner, at least the Book of Proverbs, in which לב frequently means directly the understanding. Far more intelligible and consistent is the conjecture of Mendel Stern, to which Abrahamsohn drew my attention: כּמּים הפּנים לפנים, like water (viz., flowing water), which directs its course always forward, thus (is turned) the heart of man to man. This conjecture removes the syntactic harshness of the first member without changing the letters, and illustrates by a beautiful and excellent figure the natural impulse moving man to man. It appears, however, to us, in view of the lxx, more probable that כּמּים is abbreviated from the original כאשׁר במים (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.24.29">Pro 24:29</reference>).
entries.9fcd4401f6f1798b75170e7ec30730e4ff4baa20: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.20">Pro 27:20</reference> <div eID="gen11797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11798" type="x-p"/> The following proverb has, in common with the preceding, the catchword האדם, and the emphatic repetition of the same expression: 20 The under-world and hell are not satisfied,      And the eyes of man are not satisfied. <div eID="gen11798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11799" type="x-p"/> A Kerı̂ ואבדון is here erroneously noted by Löwenstein, Stuart, and others. The Kerı̂ to ואבדּה is here ואבדּו, which secures the right utterance of the ending, and is altogether wanting<note placement="foot">In Gesen. <hi type="italic">Lex</hi>. this אבדה stands to the present day under אבדה.</note> in many MSS (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Cod. <hi type="italic">Jaman</hi>). The stripping off of the ן from the ending ון is common in the names of persons and places (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, שׁלמה, lxx Σολομών and שׁלה); we write at pleasure either <hi type="italic">ow</hi> or <hi type="italic">oh</hi> (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, מגדּו), Olsh. §215g. אבדּה (אבדּו) of the nature of a proper name, is already found in its full form אבדּון at <reference osisRef="Prov.15.11">Pro 15:11</reference>, along with שׁאול; the two synonyms are, as was there shown, not wholly alike in the idea they present, as the underworld and realm of death, but are related to each other almost the same as Hades and Gehenna; אבדון is what is called<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Frankel, <hi type="italic">Zu dem Targum der Propheten</hi> (1872), p. 25.</note> in the Jonathan-Targum בּית אבדּנא, the place of destruction, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of the second death (מותא תנינא). The proverb places Hades and Hell on the one side, and the eyes of man on the other, on the same line in respect of their insatiableness. To this Fleischer adds the remark: cf. the Arab. al'ayn l'a taml'aha all'a altrab, nothing fills the eyes of man but at last the dust of the grave - a strikingly beautiful expression! If the dust of the grave fills the open eyes, then they are full - fearful irony! The eye is the instrument of seeing, and consequently in so far as it always looks out after and farther, it is the instrument and the representation of human covetousness. The eye is filled, is satisfied, is equivalent to: human covetousness is appeased. But first “the desire of the eye,” 1Jo 2:16, is meant in the proper sense. The eyes of men are not satisfied in looking and contemplating that which is attractive and new, and no command is more difficult to be fulfilled than that in <reference osisRef="Isa.33.15">Isa 33:15</reference>, “...that shutteth his eyes from seeing evil.” There is therefore no more inexhaustible means, <hi type="italic">impiae sepculationis</hi>, than the desire of the eyes.
entries.bdebe3bd122bad8be50fc8f978b01bbafaaa623d: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.21">Pro 27:21</reference> <div eID="gen11799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11800" type="x-p"/> There follow here two proverbs which have in common with each other the figures of the crucible and the mortar: 21 The crucible for silver and the furnace for gold,      And a man according to the measure of his praise;<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, silver and gold one values according to the result of the smelting crucible and the smelting furnace; but a man, according to the measure of public opinion, which presupposes that which is said in <reference osisRef="Prov.12.8">Pro 12:8</reference>, “according to the measure of his wisdom is a man praised.” מהלל is not a ῥῆμα μέσον like our <hi type="italic">Leumund</hi> [renown], but it is a graduated idea which denotes fame down to evil <hi type="italic">Lob</hi> [fame], which is only <hi type="italic">Lob</hi> [praise] <hi type="italic">per antiphrasin</hi>. Ewald otherwise: “according to the measure of his glorying;” or Hitzig better: “according to the measure with which he praises himself,” with the remark: “מהלל is not the act, the glorifying of self, but the object of the glorying (cf. מבטח, מדון), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, that in which he places his glory.” Böttcher something further: “one recognises him by that which he is generally wont to praise in himself and others, persons and things.” Thus the proverb is to be understood; but in connection with <reference osisRef="Prov.12.8">Pro 12:8</reference> it seems to us more probable that המלל is thought of as going forth from others, and not as from himself. In line first, <reference osisRef="Prov.17.3">Pro 17:3</reference> is repeated; the second line there is conformable to the first, according to which it should be here said that the praise of a man is for him what the crucible and the furnace is for metal. The lxx, Syr., Targ., Jerome, and the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. read לפי מהללו, and thereby obtain more concinnity. Luther accordingly translates: <div eID="gen11800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11801" type="x-p"/> A man is tried by the mouth of his praise, <div eID="gen11801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11802" type="x-p"/> As silver in the crucible and gold in the furnace. <div eID="gen11802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11803" type="x-p"/> Others even think to interpret man as the subject examining, and so they vocalize the words. Thus <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Fleischer: <hi type="italic">Qualis est catinus argento et fornax auro, talis sit homo ori a quo laudatur</hi>, so that “mouth of his praise” is equivalent to the man who praises him with his mouth. But where, as here, the language relates to relative worth, the supposition for לפי, that it denotes, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.12.8">Pro 12:8</reference>, <hi type="italic">pro ratione</hi>, is tenable. And that the mouth of him who praises is a smelting crucible for him who is praised, or that the praised shall be a crucible for the mouth of him who praises, would be a wonderful comparison. The lxx has here also an additional distich which has no place in the Heb. text.
entries.c8eddfb71d59cb35d53d17bbb21882e4d64be281: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.22">Pro 27:22</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.27.22">22</reference> Though thou bruise a fool in a mortar among grit with a pestle,      Yet would not his folly depart from him. <div eID="gen11803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11804" type="x-p"/> According to the best accredited accentuations, אם־תּכתּושׁ has <hi type="italic">Illuj</hi>. and בּמּכתּשׁ has <hi type="italic">Pazer</hi>, not <hi type="italic">Rebia</hi>, which would separate more than the <hi type="italic">Dechi</hi>, and disturb the sequence of the thoughts. The first line is long; the chief disjunctive in the sphere of the <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi> is <hi type="italic">Dechi</hi> of 'הר, this disjoins more than the <hi type="italic">Pazer</hi> of 'בּם, and this again more than the <hi type="italic">Legarmeh</hi> of את־האויל. The ה of הרפות does not belong to the stem of the word (Hitzig), but is the article; רפות (from רוּף, to shake, to break; according to Schultens, from רפת, to crumble, to cut in pieces, after the form קיטור, which is improbable) are bruised grains of corn (peeled grain, grit), here they receive this name in the act of being bruised; rightly Aquila and Theodotion, ἐν μέσῳ ἐμπτισσομένων (grains of corn in the act of being pounded or bruised), and the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. μέσον τῶν πτισανῶν.<note placement="foot">The lxx translates ἐν μέσῳ συνεδρίου, and has thereby misled the Syr., and mediately the Targum.</note> <div eID="gen11804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11805" type="x-p"/> In בּעלי (thus to be written after <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 43b, not בּעלי, as Heidenheim writes it without any authority) also the article is contained. מכתשׁ is the vessel, and the ב of בעלי is <hi type="italic">Beth instrumenti</hi>; עלי (of lifting up for the purpose of bruising) is the club, pestle (Luther: <hi type="italic">stempffel</hi> = pounder); in the Mishna, <hi type="italic">Beza</hi> i. 5, this word denotes a pounder for the cutting out of flesh. The proverb interprets itself: folly has become to the fool as a second nature, and he is not to be delivered from it by the sternest discipline, the severest means that may be tried; it is not indeed his substance (Hitzig), but an inalienable accident of his substance.
entries.cba2bf3cc8c979c15d66dfeee6cad8cf6b7fae79: <reference osisRef="Prov.27.23-Prov.27.27">Pro 27:23-27</reference> <div eID="gen11805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11806" type="x-p"/> An exhortation to rural industry, and particularly to the careful tending of cattle for breeding, forms the conclusion of the foregoing series of proverbs, in which we cannot always discern an intentional grouping. It is one of the Mashal-odes spoken of vol. i. p. 12. It consists of 11 = 4 + 7 lines. 23 Give heed to the look of thy small cattle,      Be considerate about the herds. 24 For prosperity continues not for ever;      And does the diadem continue from generation to generation? 25 (But) the hay is gone, and the after-growth appears,      And the grass of the mountains is gathered: 26 Lambs serve to clothe thee,      And goats are the price of a field. 27 And there is plenty of goats’ milk for thy nourishment,      And for the nourishment of thy house,      And subsistence for thy maidens. <div eID="gen11806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11807" type="x-p"/> The beginning directs to the fut., as is not common in these proverbs, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Pro 26:26. With ידע, to take knowledge, which is strengthened by the <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. <hi type="italic">intensivus</hi>, is interchanged שׁית לב, which means at <reference osisRef="Prov.24.32">Pro 24:32</reference> to consider well, but here, to be careful regarding anything. צאן is the small or little cattle, thus sheep and goats. Whether לעדרים (here and at <reference osisRef="Isa.17.2">Isa 17:2</reference>) contains the article is questionable (Gesen. §35. 2 A), and, since the herds are called העדרים, is not probable; thus: direct thy attention to the herds, that is, to this, that thou hast herds. פּני is the external side in general; here, the appearance which the sheep present; thus their condition as seen externally. In <reference osisRef="Prov.27.24">Pro 27:24</reference> I formerly regarded נזר as a synonym of גּז, to be understood of the produce of wool, or, with Hitzig, of the shearing of the meadow, and thus the produce of the meadow. But this interpretation of the word is untenable, and <reference osisRef="Prov.27.25">Pro 27:25</reference> provides for <reference osisRef="Prov.27.24">Pro 27:24</reference>, thus understood, no natural continuation of thought. That חסן signifies a store, fulness of possessions, property, and abundance, has already been shown under <reference osisRef="Prov.15.6">Pro 15:6</reference>; but נזר is always the mark of royal, and generally of princely dignity, and here denotes, <hi type="italic">per meton</hi>. <hi type="italic">signi pro re signata</hi>, that dignity itself. With the negative expression in 24a the interrogative in 24b is interchanged as at <reference osisRef="Job.40.9">Job 40:9</reference>, with the implied negative answer; ואם, of an oath (“and truly not,” as at <reference osisRef="Isa.62.8">Isa 62:8</reference>), presents the same thought, but with a passionate colouring here unnecessary. Rightly Fleischer: “ready money, moveable property, and on the other hand the highest positions of honour, are far more easily torn away from a man, and secure to him far less of quiet prosperity, than husbandry, viewed particularly with respect to the rearing of cattle.” In other words: the possession of treasures and of a lofty place of power and of honour has not in itself the security of everlasting duration; but rural economy, and particularly the rearing of cattle, gives security for food and clothing. The Chethı̂b לדור דור is found, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Exod.3.15">Exo 3:15</reference>; the Kerı̂ לדּור ודור substitutes the more usual form. If <reference osisRef="Prov.27.25">Pro 27:25</reference> was an independent whole (Hitzig: grass vanishes and fresh green appears, etc.), then the meaning here and onward would be that in the sphere of husbandry it is otherwise than is said in <reference osisRef="Prov.27.24">Pro 27:24</reference> : there that which is consumed renews itself, and there is an enlarging circulation. But this contrast to <reference osisRef="Prov.27.24">Pro 27:24</reference> must be expressed and formed unambiguously. The connection is rather this, that <reference osisRef="Prov.27.23">Pro 27:23</reference> commends the rearing of cattle, <reference osisRef="Prov.27.24">Pro 27:24</reference> confirms it, and 25ff. discuss what real advantages, not dependent on the accidents of public and social life, it brings. <div eID="gen11807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11808" type="x-p"/> I rejoice to agree with Fleischer in the opinion that the perfects of <reference osisRef="Prov.27.25">Pro 27:25</reference> form a complex hypothetical antecedent to <reference osisRef="Prov.27.26">Pro 27:26</reference> : <hi type="italic">Quum evanuerit gramen</hi> (<hi type="italic">sc. vetus</hi>) <hi type="italic">et apparuerint herbae recentes et collecta fuerint pabula montium, agni vestitui tuo</hi> (<hi type="italic">inservient</hi>) <hi type="italic">et pretium agri</hi> (<hi type="italic">sc. a te emendi</hi>) <hi type="italic">erunt hirci</hi>, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, then wilt thou nourish thy herds of sheep and goats with the grass on thy fields, and with the dried gathered hay; and these will yield for thee, partly immediately and partly by the money derived therefrom (viz., from the valuable goats not needed for the flocks), all that is needful for thy life. He also remarks, under גּלה, that it means to make a place void, empty (viz., to quit the place, <hi type="italic">évacuer la forteresse</hi>); hence to leave one’s fatherland or home, to wander abroad; thus, rhetorically and poetically of things and possessions: to disappear. חציר (from חצר, to be green) is hay, and דּשׁא the after-growing second crop (after-grass); thus a meadow capable of being mowed a second time is though of. עשּׂבות הרים (with <hi type="italic">Dag. dirimens</hi>, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, ענּבי <reference osisRef="Deut.32.32">Deu 32:32</reference>) are the herbage of the mountains. The time when one proceeds to sheep-shearing, <reference osisRef="Prov.27.25">Pro 27:25</reference> cannot intend to designate; it sets before us an interesting rural harvest scene, where, after a plentiful ingathering of hay, one sees the meadows again overspread with new grass (Ewald); but with us the shearing of sheep takes place in the month of May, when the warm season of the year is just at hand. The poet means in general to say, that when the hay is mown and now the herbage is grown up, and also the fodder from the mountains (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.20">Psa 106:20</reference>) has been gathered home, when thus the barns are filled with plenty, the husbandman is guaranteed against the future on all sides by his stock of cattle. חלב (from חלב, Arab. halyb, with halab) is the usual metaplastic connecting form of חלב, milk. דּי (from דּי, like חי from חי), generally connected with the genitive of the person or thing, for which anything is sufficient (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.25.16">Pro 25:16</reference>, דּיּך, to which Fleischer compares Arab. hasbuha, tassuha kifayuha), has here the genitive of the thing of which, or in which, one has enough. The complex subject-conception is limited by <hi type="italic">Rebia</hi>, and the governing דּי has the subordinated disjunctive <hi type="italic">Legarmeh</hi>. עזּים is a word of two genders (<hi type="italic">epicoenum</hi>), Gesen. §107, 1d. In וחיּים the influence of the ל still continues; one does not need to supply it meanwhile, since all that maintains and nourishes life can be called חיים (<hi type="italic">vita</hi> = <hi type="italic">victus</hi>), <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Pro 3:22. The lxx translates בּיתך by σῶν θεραπόντων, and omits (as also the Syr., but not the Syro-Hexap.) the last line as now superfluous; but that the maids attending to the cattle - by whom we particularly think of milkers - are especially mentioned, intentionally presents the figure of a well-ordered household, full of varied life and activity (Job 40:29).  <chapter eID="Prov.27"/> <div eID="gen11808" type="x-p"/>

                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The desires which work and discover themselves by the eyes, 1 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 2. 16. and other senses; for otherwise <ns0:hi>the Eyes</ns0:hi> in themselves are neither capable of satisfaction nor of dissatisfaction.</ns0:note> of man are never satisfied.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 17. 3.</ns0:note> As the fining-pot for silver <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Is appointed and used for the trial of Silver, and the detection and separation of the dross from it.</ns0:note>, and the furnace for gold, so <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a man to his praise <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>according to his Praise.</ns0:hi> The sense is, so a man is known by his Praises, either 1. By the quality of those who praise and applaud him, and as they are good or bad, so is he thought to be. Or 2. By his carriage under praises, as he carries himself either humbly and modestly with thankfulness to God, and a due sense of his own infirmities, which is the case and temper of a good man; or ambitiously and vain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gloriously taking to himself the honour which he should give to God, as ungodly men generally do in that case.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 Though thou shouldst bray a fool <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Not a natural, but a moral and wilful fool, who by long con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tinuance in sin is hardened and stupified, and so incorrigible under all the means of amendment.</ns0:note> in a mortar, among wheat with a pestil, <ns0:hi>yet</ns0:hi> will not his foolishness depart from him.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="25">25 The hay appeareth, and the tender grass sheweth it self <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">In their proper seasons. These things may be here mention<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, either 1. As the matter of his diligence. Take care that thy Hay and Grass may be well managed, and seasonably gathered for the use of thy Cattle. Or rather 2. As another Argument and encouragement to diligence, because God invites thee to it by the plentiful provisions wherewith he hath enriched the Earth for thy sake. Thou needest not compass Sea and Land for them, for God puts them into thy hand if thou wiltst but receive them.</ns0:note>, and herbs of the mountains <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Even the most barren parts afford thee their help.</ns0:note> are ga<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thered <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>are to be ga<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thered,</ns0:hi> as such passive Verbs are oft used, they are ripe and ready for the gathering. So this clause suits best with the former.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 The lambs <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> for thy cloathing <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">By their wool and skins, either used to cloath thy self with, or sold to purchase all manner of cloathing for thy self and Family.</ns0:note>, and the goats <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> the price of the field <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">By the sale whereof thou maist either pay the rent of the field which thou hirest, or purchase Fields or Lands for thy self.
